title: T1 — SIR basics
text:
library(deSolve)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 14))
pal <- c(S = "#999999", I = "#E69F00", R = "#56B4E9")

title: T1 — SIR basics
text:
The model
We track the proportions of susceptible, infected and recovered individuals:
\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta S I, \qquad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta S I - \gamma I, \qquad
\frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I .
\]
\(\beta\) is the transmission rate and \(\gamma\) the recovery rate, so the mean infectious period is \(1/\gamma\).

sir <- function(t, state, p) {
  with(as.list(c(state, p)), {
    dS <- -beta * S * I
    dI <-  beta * S * I - gamma * I
    dR <-                 gamma * I
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}

init  <- c(S = 1 - 1e-6, I = 1e-6, R = 0)
pars  <- c(beta = 2, gamma = 1)          # R0 = 2
times <- seq(0, 40, by = 0.05)

out <- as.data.frame(ode(init, times, sir, pars))


R0 <- pars["beta"] / pars["gamma"]
long <- pivot_longer(out, -time, names_to = "compartment", values_to = "proportion")

ggplot(long, aes(time, proportion, colour = compartment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1 / R0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Proportion of population", colour = NULL)







Figure 1: One epidemic, R0 = 2. Infections peak exactly when S drops to 1/R0 (dashed line).

title: T1 — SIR basics
text:
Two numbers you can check
Herd immunity threshold. \(dI/dt > 0\) exactly when \(S > \gamma/\beta = 1/R_0\). So the epidemic peaks when a fraction \(1 - 1/R_0\) is no longer susceptible.

c(S_at_peak = out$S[which.max(out$I)], one_over_R0 = unname(1 / R0))

  S_at_peak one_over_R0 
   0.496625    0.500000 


Final size. The fraction \(Z\) ever infected solves \(Z = 1 - e^{-R_0 Z}\).

Z <- uniroot(function(z) z - (1 - exp(-R0 * z)), c(1e-6, 1))$root
c(simulated = tail(out$R, 1), theory = Z)

simulated    theory 
0.7968124 0.7968113 


Note that \(Z > 1 - 1/R_0\): the epidemic overshoots the herd immunity threshold.

title: T1 — SIR basics
text:
Adding births and deaths
With births and deaths at rate \(\mu\), new susceptibles keep arriving and the infection can become endemic:
\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = \mu - \beta S I - \mu S, \qquad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta S I - (\gamma + \mu) I, \qquad
\frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I - \mu R .
\]
Now \(R_0 = \beta / (\gamma + \mu)\), and the endemic equilibrium is \(S^* = 1/R_0\), \(I^* = \mu (R_0 - 1) / \beta\).

sir_demo <- function(t, state, p) {
  with(as.list(c(state, p)), {
    dS <- mu - beta * S * I - mu * S
    dI <- beta * S * I - (gamma + mu) * I
    dR <- gamma * I - mu * R
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}
pars_d <- c(beta = 3, gamma = 1, mu = 0.02)
out_d  <- as.data.frame(ode(c(S = 0.99, I = 0.01, R = 0), seq(0, 600, 0.1),
                            sir_demo, pars_d))
R0_d   <- with(as.list(pars_d), beta / (gamma + mu))
eq     <- with(as.list(pars_d), c(S = 1 / R0_d, I = mu * (R0_d - 1) / beta))


ggplot(out_d, aes(S, I)) +
  geom_path(colour = "#E69F00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("point", x = eq["S"], y = eq["I"], colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Susceptible S", y = "Infected I (log scale)")







Figure 2: Phase plane: with births, the epidemic spirals into the endemic equilibrium (red point).

title: T2 — Chance: epidemic takeoff and evolutionary rescue
text:
library(deSolve)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 14))
set.seed(1)
The idea. A single infected person entering a susceptible population, and a single resistant bacterium in a patient on antibiotics, are the same problem. Each is one lineage that grows on average but can be lost by chance while it is still rare. Below we simulate both and compare them with one formula.

title: T2 — Chance: epidemic takeoff and evolutionary rescue
section: Part A · Does the epidemic take off?
text:
Part A · Does the epidemic take off?

A stochastic SIR model (Gillespie algorithm)
The ODE in T1 follows proportions and assumes an infinite population. Here we follow individual events in a population of \(N\):



Event
Rate
Change




infection
\(\beta S I / N\)
\(S \to S-1,\; I \to I+1\)


recovery
\(\gamma I\)
\(I \to I-1,\; R \to R+1\)



The Gillespie algorithm repeats the following. Draw the waiting time to the next event from an exponential distribution with the total rate. Then pick which event happens, with probability proportional to its rate.

gillespie_sir <- function(N, beta, gamma, I0 = 1, tmax = Inf) {
  S <- N - I0; I <- I0; R <- 0; t <- 0
  n_max <- 2 * N + 1                    # every individual is infected and recovers at most once
  rec <- matrix(NA_real_, n_max, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("time", "S", "I", "R")))
  k <- 1; rec[k, ] <- c(t, S, I, R)
  while (I > 0 && t < tmax) {
    a_inf <- beta * S * I / N
    a_rec <- gamma * I
    a_tot <- a_inf + a_rec
    t <- t + rexp(1, a_tot)             # waiting time
    if (runif(1) < a_inf / a_tot) {     # which event?
      S <- S - 1; I <- I + 1
    } else {
      I <- I - 1; R <- R + 1
    }
    k <- k + 1; rec[k, ] <- c(t, S, I, R)
  }
  as.data.frame(rec[1:k, , drop = FALSE])
}


N <- 1000; gamma <- 1; R0 <- 2
runs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:20, function(i)
  cbind(gillespie_sir(N, beta = R0 * gamma, gamma = gamma), run = i)))

sir_ode <- function(t, x, p) with(as.list(c(x, p)),
  list(c(-beta * S * I, beta * S * I - gamma * I, gamma * I)))
ode_out <- as.data.frame(ode(c(S = 1 - 1/N, I = 1/N, R = 0), seq(0, 25, 0.05),
                             sir_ode, c(beta = R0 * gamma, gamma = gamma)))

ggplot(runs, aes(time, I, group = run)) +
  geom_step(colour = "#E69F00", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = ode_out, aes(time, I * N), inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Number infected")







Figure 1: 20 stochastic epidemics started by one infected individual (N = 1000, R0 = 2), with the ODE solution in black. Many runs die out almost immediately.







Takeoff probability
Early on, \(S \approx N\). Each infected person then infects others at rate \(\beta\) until they recover at rate \(\gamma\). Each next event is an infection with probability \(\beta/(\beta+\gamma)\), so the number of secondary cases is geometric with mean \(R_0\). Haldane’s argument (below) then gives
\[
P(\text{takeoff}) = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0} \quad (R_0 > 1).
\]






Haldane’s argument in three lines





Let \(\eta\) be the probability that a lineage eventually dies out. A lineage dies out only if all of its offspring lineages die out, so \(\eta = \sum_k P(k \text{ offspring})\, \eta^k = G(\eta)\).

Geometric offspring with mean \(R_0\): \(G(\eta) = 1/(1 + R_0(1-\eta))\), so \(\eta = 1/R_0\).
Poisson offspring with mean \(R_0\): \(G(\eta) = e^{R_0(\eta - 1)}\), which has no closed-form solution. Solve it numerically.





# Faster version: stop as soon as the outcome is clear
takeoff <- function(N, R0, gamma = 1, threshold = 0.1 * N) {
  S <- N - 1; I <- 1
  while (I > 0 && (N - S) < threshold) {
    a_inf <- R0 * gamma * S * I / N
    if (runif(1) < a_inf / (a_inf + gamma * I)) { S <- S - 1; I <- I + 1 } else I <- I - 1
  }
  I > 0
}

R0_vec <- seq(0.5, 3, by = 0.25)
reps   <- 500
p_sim  <- sapply(R0_vec, function(R0) mean(replicate(reps, takeoff(N = 1000, R0 = R0))))

p_poisson <- sapply(R0_vec, function(R0) {
  if (R0 <= 1) return(0)
  1 - uniroot(function(e) e - exp(R0 * (e - 1)), c(0, 1 - 1e-6))$root
})


df <- data.frame(R0 = R0_vec, sim = p_sim,
                 geometric = pmax(0, 1 - 1 / R0_vec), poisson = p_poisson)
ggplot(df, aes(R0)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = geometric), linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#56B4E9") +
  geom_line(aes(y = poisson), linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(y = sim), size = 3, colour = "#E69F00") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = expression(R[0]), y = "P(major outbreak)")







Figure 2: Probability that one infection starts a major outbreak. Points: Gillespie SIR. Solid: 1 − 1/R0 (geometric offspring). Dashed: what Poisson offspring would give.





Same mean, different variance, different answer. Superspreading (high variance in secondary cases) makes outbreaks less likely to take off. That is the starting point for a project.

title: T2 — Chance: epidemic takeoff and evolutionary rescue
section: Part B · Does resistance rescue the population?
text:
Part B · Does resistance rescue the population?
A population of \(N\) sensitive bacteria is treated, and each generation it shrinks by a factor \(1 - r\). Each new cell is resistant with probability \(u\). Resistant cells grow by a factor \(1 + s\) per generation. Offspring numbers are Poisson.

rescue <- function(N, r, s, u, max_gen = 20000, threshold = 2 / s) {
  wt <- N; mut <- 0
  for (g in 1:max_gen) {
    wt  <- rpois(1, wt * (1 - r))
    mut <- rpois(1, mut * (1 + s))
    new <- rbinom(1, wt, u)            # mutation among new offspring
    wt  <- wt - new; mut <- mut + new
    if (wt == 0 && mut == 0) return(0) # extinction
    if (mut > threshold) return(1)     # resistant lineage established: rescue
  }
  NA
}

N <- 1e4; u <- 1e-5; s <- 0.02
r_vec  <- c(0.001, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05)
p_resc <- sapply(r_vec, function(r) mean(replicate(300, rescue(N, r, s, u)), na.rm = TRUE))

Theory. While it declines, the sensitive population produces about \(N/r\) cells in total, so about \(Nu/r\) mutants. Each of them escapes loss with probability \(\approx 2s\) (Haldane, for Poisson offspring with mean \(1 + s\)). The number of successful mutants is then roughly Poisson, so
\[
P(\text{rescue}) \approx 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{2 N u s}{r}\right) \qquad \text{(Orr \& Unckless 2014).}
\]

r_fine <- 10^seq(-3, log10(0.05), length.out = 100)
ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(r_fine, 1 - exp(-2 * N * u * s / r_fine)), linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#56B4E9") +
  geom_point(aes(r_vec, p_resc), size = 3, colour = "#E69F00") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Strength of treatment r (log scale)", y = "P(rescue by resistance)")







Figure 3: Probability that resistance evolves before the treated population goes extinct. Points: simulation. Line: 1 − exp(−2Nus/r).

title: T2 — Chance: epidemic takeoff and evolutionary rescue
text:
The one rule behind both
For a rare lineage whose mean offspring number is just above 1,
\[
P(\text{establishment}) \;\approx\; \frac{2\,(\text{mean} - 1)}{\text{variance}} .
\]

Resistant mutant: mean \(1 + s\), Poisson variance \(\approx 1\), which gives \(2s\).
New epidemic: mean \(R_0\), geometric variance \(R_0(1+R_0) \approx 2\), which gives \(R_0 - 1 \approx 1 - 1/R_0\).

title: T2 — Chance: epidemic takeoff and evolutionary rescue
text:
Exercises

In Part A, how does the takeoff probability change if you start with \(I_0 = 5\)? Predict first: with independent lineages, \(P = 1 - (1/R_0)^{I_0}\).
In Part B, plot \(P(\text{rescue})\) against \(N\) on a log axis. Where is the switch from “almost never” to “almost always”?
Start Part B with 5 resistant cells already present (standing variation). When does this matter more than new mutations?
Rerun Part B with \(N = 1000\) and \(u = 10^{-4}\). That keeps \(2Nus\) the same, so the theory curve does not change, but the simulations fall below it at small \(r\). Why? Hint: the theory assumes the sensitive population declines deterministically. Compare \(r\) with \(1/N\).

title: T4 — Within-host dynamics and drug resistance
text:
library(deSolve)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 14))
The question. A patient with a chronic viral infection starts drug treatment. The virus population already contains a few drug-resistant mutants. Which dose suppresses the infection, and which dose selects for resistance instead?

title: T4 — Within-host dynamics and drug resistance
text:
The target-cell model
Inside the host, uninfected target cells \(T\) are infected by free virus \(V\) and become infected cells \(I\). Infected cells produce new virus and die (Perelson 2002, Nat Rev Immunol; Nowak & May 2000):
\[
\frac{dT}{dt} = \lambda - dT - \beta T V, \qquad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta T V - \delta I, \qquad
\frac{dV}{dt} = p I - c V .
\]
It has the same structure as SIR: \(T\) plays the role of susceptibles. The within-host basic reproduction number counts the infected cells produced by one infected cell in a fresh host:
\[
R_0 = \frac{\beta\,\lambda\,p}{d\,\delta\,c}.
\]

title: T4 — Within-host dynamics and drug resistance
text:
Drug, resistance and mutation

The drug blocks infection: \(\beta \to (1 - \varepsilon)\beta\), with dose response \(\varepsilon(D) = D/(D + \mathrm{IC}_{50})\).
The resistant mutant \(M\) pays a fitness cost \(\kappa\), so \(\beta_M = (1 - \kappa)\beta\). It needs a \(\rho\)-fold higher dose for the same effect: \(\varepsilon_M(D) = D/(D + \rho\,\mathrm{IC}_{50})\).
Each wild-type infection produces a mutant with probability \(u\).


wh <- function(t, x, p) {
  with(as.list(c(x, p)), {
    eW <- D / (D + IC50)
    eM <- D / (D + rho * IC50)
    infW <- (1 - eW) * beta * T * VW
    infM <- (1 - eM) * (1 - kappa) * beta * T * VM
    dT  <- lambda - d * T - infW - infM
    dIW <- (1 - u) * infW - delta * IW
    dIM <- u * infW + infM - delta * IM
    dVW <- p * IW - c * VW
    dVM <- p * IM - c * VM
    list(c(dT, dIW, dIM, dVW, dVM))
  })
}

# Illustrative HIV-like values (per mL, per day), in the range reviewed by Perelson (2002)
pars <- c(lambda = 1e4, d = 0.01, beta = 2e-7, delta = 1, p = 1000, c = 23,
          kappa = 0.2, rho = 10, u = 3e-5, IC50 = 1, D = 0)
R0  <- with(as.list(pars), beta * lambda * p / (d * delta * c))
R0M <- (1 - pars[["kappa"]]) * R0
c(R0_wildtype = R0, R0_mutant = R0M)

R0_wildtype   R0_mutant 
   8.695652    6.956522 


First, let the untreated infection settle to its chronic equilibrium. Mutants are already present at a low frequency (mutation–selection balance).

x0  <- c(T = 1e6, IW = 0, IM = 0, VW = 1e-3, VM = 0)
pre <- ode(x0, seq(0, 1000, 1), wh, pars)
eq  <- pre[nrow(pre), -1]
signif(eq, 3)

       T       IW       IM       VW       VM 
1.15e+05 8.85e+03 1.33e+00 3.85e+05 5.77e+01

title: T4 — Within-host dynamics and drug resistance
text:
Three doses that matter
Under the drug, each strain has an effective reproduction number:
\[
R_W(D) = R_0\,\frac{\mathrm{IC}_{50}}{D + \mathrm{IC}_{50}}, \qquad
R_M(D) = (1-\kappa)R_0\,\frac{\rho\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}}{D + \rho\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}} .
\]
Setting these equal to 1, or to each other, gives three simple thresholds:

\(D_x = \dfrac{\rho\kappa}{\rho(1-\kappa) - 1}\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}\). Above this dose the mutant has the larger \(R\), so resistance is favoured. As in T3, the strain with the larger \(R\) wins the competition for target cells.
\(D_W = (R_0 - 1)\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}\). Above this dose the wild type cannot persist even on its own.
\(D_M = \rho\big((1-\kappa)R_0 - 1\big)\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}\). Above this dose nothing persists.

Between \(D_W\) and \(D_M\) the drug removes the wild type but not the mutant. This is the classical mutant selection window. The figure shows it is only part of the range where resistance wins.

IC50 <- pars[["IC50"]]; rho <- pars[["rho"]]; kappa <- pars[["kappa"]]
Dx <- rho * kappa / (rho * (1 - kappa) - 1) * IC50
DW <- (R0 - 1) * IC50
DM <- rho * (R0M - 1) * IC50
round(c(D_x = Dx, D_W = DW, D_M = DM), 2)

  D_x   D_W   D_M 
 0.29  7.70 59.57 

doses <- 10^seq(-1, 3, length.out = 200)
reff  <- rbind(data.frame(dose = doses, R = R0 * IC50 / (doses + IC50), virus = "wild type"),
               data.frame(dose = doses, R = R0M * rho * IC50 / (doses + rho * IC50), virus = "resistant"))
ggplot(reff, aes(dose, R, colour = virus)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = DW, xmax = DM, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Dx, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`wild type` = "#56B4E9", resistant = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = expression("Dose (multiples of " * IC[50] * ")"),
       y = "Effective R (log)", colour = NULL)







Figure 1: Effective reproduction numbers under treatment. Resistance is favoured above D_x; the classical selection window (shaded) lies between D_W and D_M.

title: T4 — Within-host dynamics and drug resistance
text:
Simulating treatment

treat <- function(D, days = 365) {
  as.data.frame(ode(eq, seq(0, days, 0.5), wh, replace(pars, "D", D)))
}
tc   <- treat(D = 20)
long <- pivot_longer(tc[, c("time", "VW", "VM")], -time, names_to = "virus", values_to = "V")
ggplot(long, aes(time, pmax(V, 1e-3), colour = virus)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(VW = "#56B4E9", VM = "#D55E00"),
                      labels = c(VM = "resistant", VW = "wild type")) +
  labs(x = "Days of treatment", y = "Virus per mL (log)", colour = NULL)







Figure 2: Treatment at 20 × IC50, inside the window. Both strains crash at first because target cells are depleted when treatment starts. Then the resistant strain rebounds as target cells recover. Values below 10^-3 are drawn at 10^-3.





At its lowest point the resistant virus is at 2.4e-05 virions per mL. Keep that number in mind for the warning box below.

scan <- do.call(rbind, lapply(10^seq(-1, 3, length.out = 61), function(D) {
  last <- tail(treat(D), 1)
  data.frame(dose = D, virus = c("wild type", "resistant"), V = c(last$VW, last$VM))
}))


ggplot(scan, aes(dose, pmax(V, 1e-3), colour = virus)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = DW, xmax = DM, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Dx, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`wild type` = "#56B4E9", resistant = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = expression("Dose (multiples of " * IC[50] * ")"),
       y = "Virus per mL after 1 year (log)", colour = NULL)







Figure 3: Viral load after one year of treatment. Resistance takes over from D_x (dashed) up to roughly D_M. Near D_M the mutant grows so slowly that it has not yet rebounded after one year. Values below 10^-3 are drawn at 10^-3.











Where the deterministic model lies



In this ODE the resistant strain is never exactly zero. So whenever resistance is favoured it always rebounds, even from the tiny minimum computed above. A real patient cannot carry a fraction of a virion. Whether resistance actually appears is an evolutionary rescue problem: will a mutant arise and escape stochastic loss before the wild type is gone? Go back to T2.

title: Day 1 — Two ways to model an outbreak
text:
10:30 · Lecture 2 — When chance decides
The first infected person in a new population and the first resistant bacterium in a treated patient are in the same situation. Both are a single lineage that grows on average but can easily be lost by chance.

Branching processes: each individual leaves a random number of “offspring” (infections, daughter cells).
Haldane (1927): the extinction probability \(\eta\) solves \(\eta = G(\eta)\), where \(G\) is the offspring generating function.
Epidemic takeoff: in SIR, \(P(\text{takeoff}) = 1 - 1/R_0\).
Evolution of resistance (evolutionary rescue): a population under treatment declines at rate \(r\), and resistant mutants arise at rate \(u\) and grow at rate \(s\).

Establishment probability of one mutant \(\approx 2s\).
Rescue probability \(\approx 1 - \exp(-2Nus/r)\) (Orr & Unckless 2014).

The unifying rule: \(P(\text{establish}) \approx 2 \times (\text{mean} - 1) / \text{variance}\) of the offspring number.

title: Day 2 — Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
09:00 · Lecture 3
Between hosts: which strain wins?

Two strains with complete cross-immunity, in a population with births and deaths.
A rare mutant grows when \(\beta_m S^* > \gamma_m + \mu\). At the resident equilibrium \(S^* = 1/R_0^{\text{res}}\), so the strain with the larger \(R_0\) wins, even if it transmits less per contact.
Virulence trade-off: if \(\beta(\alpha) \propto \sqrt{\alpha}\), then \(R_0\) is maximised at \(\alpha^* = \gamma + \mu\), an intermediate virulence.
A mutant strain arising during one epidemic must appear early, while \(S\) is still high (branching process again).

Within a host: virus, cells and drugs

Target-cell model (Perelson 2002): \(T \to I \to V\), with a within-host \(R_0 = \beta \lambda p / (d\,\delta\,c)\).
The drug blocks infection with efficacy \(\varepsilon\). The wild type is suppressed if \(\varepsilon > 1 - 1/R_0\).
A resistant mutant pays a fitness cost but tolerates the drug better. Three simple dose thresholds follow: where resistance becomes favoured (\(D_x\)), where the wild type alone is stopped (\(D_W\)), and where everything is stopped (\(D_M\)). Between \(D_W\) and \(D_M\) lies the classical mutant selection window.
Link to Day 1: whether resistance actually appears is a rescue problem. Deterministic models get this wrong.

Frame the lecture: same competition logic at two scales. Pitch 2 follows right after this lecture, so remind them to note down which parts are relevant for their project.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
The question
A mutant strain appears in a population where a resident strain is endemic.

Recovery from either strain protects against both (complete cross-immunity).
The two strains compete for the same susceptible hosts.

When does the mutant take over?

Examples: SARS-CoV-2 variants replacing each other; seasonal influenza lineages; myxoma virus in Australian rabbits.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
section: Two strains, one pool of susceptibles
text:
Two strains, one pool of susceptibles
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt}   &= \mu - (\beta_1 I_1 + \beta_2 I_2) S - \mu S \\[4pt]
\frac{dI_i}{dt} &= \beta_i S I_i - (\gamma_i + \mu) I_i \qquad i = 1, 2 \\[4pt]
\frac{dR}{dt}   &= \gamma_1 I_1 + \gamma_2 I_2 - \mu R
\end{aligned}
\]

Each strain alone: \(R_0^{(i)} = \dfrac{\beta_i}{\gamma_i + \mu}\), with endemic equilibrium \(S^* = 1/R_0^{(i)}\).

This is the SIR with demography from Lecture 1, just with two I compartments. Ask: why do we need births for this question? (Without births there is no endemic resident to invade.)

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Invasion analysis
While the mutant is rare, the resident sits at its equilibrium, \(S^* = 1/R_0^{(1)}\).
The mutant’s per-capita growth rate is then
\[
\lambda = \beta_2 S^* - (\gamma_2 + \mu)
\;=\; (\gamma_2 + \mu)\left(\frac{R_0^{(2)}}{R_0^{(1)}} - 1\right).
\]







The mutant invades if and only if \(R_0^{(2)} > R_0^{(1)}\).






It does not have to transmit faster. It only needs more secondary infections over its whole infectious period.

Derive on the board: substitute S* = (gamma1+mu)/beta1. This is the “invasion fitness” idea from adaptive dynamics: grow the rare type in the environment set by the resident.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Where \(S^*\) comes from
Strain 1 alone, at its endemic equilibrium. Set \(dI_1/dt = 0\) with \(I_1 > 0\):
\[
\beta_1 S^* I_1 - (\gamma_1 + \mu) I_1 = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
S^* = \frac{\gamma_1 + \mu}{\beta_1} = \frac{1}{R_0^{(1)}}
\]

Now add one rare mutant. It barely changes \(S\), so its growth rate is
\[
\frac{1}{I_2}\frac{dI_2}{dt} = \beta_2 S^* - (\gamma_2 + \mu)
= (\gamma_2 + \mu)\left(\frac{\beta_2}{\gamma_2 + \mu}\cdot\frac{1}{R_0^{(1)}} - 1\right)
\]


and \(\beta_2/(\gamma_2 + \mu) = R_0^{(2)}\), which gives \(\lambda = (\gamma_2+\mu)\left(R_0^{(2)}/R_0^{(1)} - 1\right)\).
Invasion fitness: let the resident set the environment (here \(S^*\)), then ask whether the rare type grows in it.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Why only one strain survives
Each strain alone would push susceptibles down to its own level:
\[
S^*_1 = 1/R_0^{(1)}, \qquad S^*_2 = 1/R_0^{(2)}
\]


Strain \(i\) grows only if \(S > S^*_i\).
The strain with the larger \(R_0\) pushes \(S\) below the level the other strain needs.
So the other strain declines. Both can only coexist if \(S^*_1 = S^*_2\) exactly.



This is competitive exclusion, the same logic as resource competition in ecology. The strain that tolerates the lowest resource level wins. Here the resource is susceptible hosts.
Coexistence needs something more: partial cross-immunity, different host groups, or space. That is good project material.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
section: Lower transmission, but it still wins
text:
Lower transmission, but it still wins


Initial slope of the mutant matches lambda = 0.098 exactly (checked in T3). Competitive exclusion: with one shared resource (S) only one strain persists.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Quick check
Strain 2 transmits twice as fast as strain 1, but infected hosts recover three times faster.
Same \(\mu\), with \(\mu \ll \gamma\).
Who wins?

\[
\frac{R_0^{(2)}}{R_0^{(1)}} \approx \frac{2\beta_1 / 3\gamma_1}{\beta_1/\gamma_1} = \frac{2}{3} < 1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{the resident wins.}
\]

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
section: So why don’t pathogens maximise \(R_0\) without limit?
text:
So why don’t pathogens maximise \(R_0\) without limit?
Pathogens that replicate faster

transmit better: \(\beta\) goes up, but
harm or kill their host sooner: virulence \(\alpha\) goes up, which shortens the infectious period.

\[
R_0(\alpha) = \frac{\beta(\alpha)}{\gamma + \mu + \alpha}
\]

This is the transmission–virulence trade-off (Anderson & May 1982; Alizon et al. 2009).

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
section: A simple trade-off gives intermediate virulence
text:
A simple trade-off gives intermediate virulence


Take \(\beta(\alpha) = b\sqrt{\alpha}\):
\[
\frac{dR_0}{d\alpha} = 0
\;\Rightarrow\;
\alpha^* = \gamma + \mu
\]
Optimal virulence equals the rate at which hosts clear the infection or die of other causes.
Since the largest \(R_0\) wins, evolution should drive \(\alpha \to \alpha^*\).

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Finding \(\alpha^*\)
Write \(c = \gamma + \mu\), so \(R_0(\alpha) = b\,\sqrt{\alpha}\,/\,(c + \alpha)\). Use the quotient rule:

\[
\frac{dR_0}{d\alpha}
= b\,\frac{\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\alpha}}\,(c + \alpha) - \sqrt{\alpha}}{(c + \alpha)^2}
\]


This is zero when the numerator is zero. Multiply by \(2\sqrt{\alpha}\):
\[
(c + \alpha) - 2\alpha = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\alpha^* = c = \gamma + \mu
\]


Interpretation: at the optimum, the pathogen kills its host at the same rate as the host clears the infection or dies of other causes. A different trade-off shape gives a different \(\alpha^*\), which is why measuring the trade-off matters.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Evidence, and caveats
Myxoma virus in Australia (released 1950)

The original strain killed more than 99% of infected rabbits.
Within a few years, strains of intermediate virulence dominated (Fenner & Ratcliffe 1965; Kerr et al. 2012).


Caveats

The shape of the trade-off is hard to measure, and often assumed rather than shown (Alizon et al. 2009).
Hosts evolve too: myxoma virulence later increased again as rabbits became resistant (Kerr et al. 2017).
With spatial structure or superinfection, the “maximise \(R_0\)” rule can fail.


Good project material: any of these caveats is a project. Point to the project menu, family C.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
section: A variant arising during one epidemic
text:
A variant arising during one epidemic
There is no endemic equilibrium now. Mutants arise at rate \(u \times\) (new infections) and must survive the branching phase from Day 1:
\[
P(\text{variant establishes}) \approx 1 - \exp\!\left(-\int u N \beta S I \;\max\!\Big[0,\; 1 - \tfrac{1}{R_0^{(m)} S(t)}\Big]\, dt\right)
\]


The establishment term needs \(R_0^{(m)} S(t) > 1\), so a variant must arise early, before \(S\) has dropped.
Many infections help (more chances), but they also use up \(S\).


This is T3 Part C. It is an approximation (S keeps falling while the lineage is small); checking it with Gillespie is a good project.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Bridge: resistance spreading between hosts




Part 1’s two-strain model, with treatment:

\(I_S\): infected with a drug-sensitive strain. Treated, so they recover fast.
\(I_R\): infected with a resistant strain, which treatment does not help.
Emergence: resistance arises within treated hosts, \(I_S \to I_R\).

Treatment lowers \(R_0\) of the sensitive strain, so by Part 1 it hands the advantage to the resistant strain.


But where does the \(I_S \to I_R\) arrow come from? From evolution inside one patient. That is Part 2.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
The target-cell model
\[
\frac{dT}{dt} = \lambda - dT - \beta T V, \qquad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta T V - \delta I, \qquad
\frac{dV}{dt} = p I - c V
\]

Within-host basic reproduction number:
\[
R_0 = \underbrace{\frac{\lambda}{d}}_{\text{target cells}}\;\cdot\;
\underbrace{\beta}_{\text{infection}}\;\cdot\;
\underbrace{\frac{p}{\delta}}_{\text{virions per cell}}\;\cdot\;
\underbrace{\frac{1}{c}}_{\text{virion lifetime}}
\]
The chronic infection settles at \(T^* = T_0/R_0\), just as \(S^* = 1/R_0\) in SIR.

Perelson 2002 Nat Rev Immunol; Nowak & May 2000 “Virus Dynamics”. Read R0 as a chain: one infected cell makes p/delta virions, each lives 1/c and infects at rate beta*T0.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Within-host \(R_0\), step by step
Follow one infected cell in a fresh host, with \(T = T_0 = \lambda/d\) target cells:


It lives on average \(1/\delta\) days and produces \(p\) virions per day: \(p/\delta\) virions.
Each virion lives \(1/c\) days and infects at rate \(\beta T_0\): \(\beta T_0 / c\) infected cells per virion.



Multiply:
\[
R_0 = \frac{p}{\delta} \cdot \frac{\beta T_0}{c} = \frac{\beta\,\lambda\,p}{d\,\delta\,c}
\]


With HIV-like values (\(\beta = 2\times10^{-7}\), \(\lambda = 10^4\), \(p = 1000\), \(d = 0.01\), \(\delta = 1\), \(c = 23\)):
\[
R_0 = \frac{2\times10^{-7}\cdot 10^4 \cdot 1000}{0.01 \cdot 1 \cdot 23} \approx 8.7
\]

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
The chronic infection
At equilibrium, \(dV/dt = 0\) gives \(V^* = p I^*/c\). Insert this into \(dI/dt = 0\):
\[
\beta T^* \frac{p I^*}{c} = \delta I^*
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
T^* = \frac{\delta c}{\beta p} = \frac{T_0}{R_0}
\]


This is the same as \(S^* = 1/R_0\) in SIR: the virus depletes target cells until each infected cell just replaces itself.
With \(R_0 \approx 8.7\), only about 11% of target cells remain in chronic infection.



Keep this in mind: when treatment starts, target cells are depleted. That will matter in a few slides.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Drug and resistance

The drug blocks infection: \(\beta \to (1 - \varepsilon)\beta\), with \(\varepsilon(D) = \dfrac{D}{D + \mathrm{IC}_{50}}\).
The resistant mutant

pays a fitness cost \(\kappa\): \(\beta_M = (1 - \kappa)\beta\),
needs a \(\rho\)-fold higher dose: \(\varepsilon_M(D) = \dfrac{D}{D + \rho\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}}\),
arises with probability \(u\) per infection.



Before treatment, mutants are already present at mutation–selection balance. That is standing variation, as in the Day 1 exercise.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
How many mutants before treatment?
At the chronic equilibrium, the wild type exactly replaces itself. The mutant, with cost \(\kappa\), replaces only a fraction \(1 - \kappa\) of itself, and is resupplied by mutation:
\[
\frac{dI_M}{dt} = \underbrace{u\,\delta I_W}_{\text{new mutants}} + \underbrace{(1-\kappa)\,\delta I_M}_{\text{own replication}} - \underbrace{\delta I_M}_{\text{death}} = 0
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{I_M}{I_W} = \frac{u}{\kappa}}
\qquad \text{mutation–selection balance}
\]


Here: \(u/\kappa = 3\times10^{-5}/0.2 = 1.5\times10^{-4}\). In the simulation, 1.5^{-4}.
With about \(10^4\) infected cells per mL, that is roughly one resistant infected cell per mL before treatment even starts.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Three doses that matter
Effective reproduction numbers under treatment:
\[
R_W(D) = \frac{R_0\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}}{D + \mathrm{IC}_{50}}, \qquad
R_M(D) = \frac{(1-\kappa)R_0\,\rho\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}}{D + \rho\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}}
\]










Threshold
Meaning
Formula
Here




\(D_x\)
resistance favoured (\(R_M > R_W\))
\(\rho\kappa / (\rho(1-\kappa)-1)\cdot\mathrm{IC}_{50}\)
0.29


\(D_W\)
wild type cannot persist
\((R_0 - 1)\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}\)
7.7


\(D_M\)
nothing persists
\(\rho\big((1-\kappa)R_0 - 1\big)\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}\)
59.6



Illustrative HIV-like parameters: \(R_0 =\) 8.7, \(\kappa = 0.2\), \(\rho = 10\).

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Deriving the thresholds
\(D_W\), the wild type cannot persist: set \(R_W(D) = 1\):
\[
\frac{R_0\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}}{D + \mathrm{IC}_{50}} = 1
\;\Rightarrow\; D + \mathrm{IC}_{50} = R_0\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}
\;\Rightarrow\; D_W = (R_0 - 1)\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}
\]
\(D_M\) is the same calculation with \((1-\kappa)R_0\) and \(\rho\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}\).

\(D_x\), resistance is favoured: set \(R_W(D) = R_M(D)\) and cancel \(R_0\) (write \(\mathrm{IC}_{50} = 1\)):
\[
\frac{1}{D + 1} = \frac{(1-\kappa)\rho}{D + \rho}
\;\Rightarrow\; D + \rho = (1-\kappa)\rho\,(D + 1)
\;\Rightarrow\; D_x = \frac{\rho\kappa}{\rho(1-\kappa) - 1}
\]



\(D_x\) is small when the cost \(\kappa\) is small: cheap resistance is favoured by almost any dose.
\(D_x\) exists only if \(\rho(1-\kappa) > 1\), i.e. resistance must outweigh its cost.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
section: The selection window is only part of the story
text:
The selection window is only part of the story


Classical MSW (Drlica): between the MIC of the wild type and the MIC of the mutant. But in competition, the mutant already wins above D_x, because it has the larger R (same logic as Part 1). Below D_W the wild type would persist alone, but it is outcompeted.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Treatment inside the window: 20 × IC50

Both strains crash first, because target cells are depleted. The resistant strain then rebounds as target cells recover.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Why both strains crash first
At the start of treatment, target cells are at \(T^* = T_0/R_0\), not \(T_0\). The effective reproduction number of the mutant is therefore
\[
R_M(D)\cdot\frac{T^*}{T_0} = \frac{R_M(D)}{R_0}
\]

At \(D = 20\,\mathrm{IC}_{50}\): \(R_M = 2.32\), so \(R_M / R_0 = 0.27 < 1\), and the mutant declines too.



Target cells recover at rate \(d = 0.01\)/day, a time scale of months.
Once \(T/T_0 > 1/R_M(D)\), the mutant grows again.
The deterministic model lets it regrow from a tiny fraction of a virion. A real patient may have lost every resistant virus during the dip.

In this model, the first weeks of treatment are when resistance is most vulnerable. Whether that holds for real patients is a question for a stochastic model (project!).

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
section: Outcome after one year, by dose
text: Outcome after one year, by dose

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Where the deterministic model lies
At its lowest point, the resistant virus in the ODE is at 2.4e-05 virions per mL, and then it rebounds.

A real patient cannot carry a fraction of a virion.

In the ODE, resistance is never truly zero, so whenever it is favoured it always wins.
In reality a resistant mutant must arise and escape stochastic loss before the wild type is gone.



That is evolutionary rescue from Day 1:
\[
P(\text{resistance}) \approx 1 - \exp\big(-\text{(mutants produced)} \times P(\text{establish})\big)
\]

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
What this means for treatment

Combination therapy (e.g. HIV): resistance needs several mutations, so the “mutants produced” term collapses.
Adherence: missed doses move the drug concentration through the window, again and again.
Hit hard, or contain? Aggressive treatment removes competitors of resistant cells. Whether it helps or hurts is an open debate (Read, Day & Huijben 2011, PNAS).


Read et al. 2011 “The evolution of drug resistance and the curious orthodoxy of aggressive chemotherapy”. Link back to the Uecker/Otto/Hermisson point from the ER deck: competition release.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Hit hard, or contain?





Top: maximum dose removes the sensitive cells, and with them the competitors of the resistant cells. Bottom: treat only enough to keep the tumour or infection in check, and sensitive cells keep resistant cells suppressed. This is the idea behind adaptive therapy in cancer.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Competition changes the answer




Rescue probability against treatment strength \(r\) (Uecker, Otto & Hermisson 2014):

No competition (squares): stronger treatment always lowers the chance of resistance, as on Day 1.
Sensitive and resistant cells compete (circles): the curve is no longer monotonic. Over a range of \(r\), stronger treatment makes resistance more likely, because it frees resources for the resistant cells.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Treatment strategies in a hospital





Angst et al. (2021) ran an in vitro hospital: wells of bacteria are “patients”, admitted, treated and discharged each day. They compared no treatment, monotherapy, combination therapy, cycling and mixing. In their setup combination therapy (F) kept resistance lowest.

title: Pathogen evolution, between and within hosts
text:
Summary

Between hosts: the strain with the larger \(R_0\) invades and wins. With a transmission–virulence trade-off that means intermediate virulence, \(\alpha^* = \gamma + \mu\).
Within a host: the same competition, now for target cells. Resistance is favoured above \(D_x\), and only doses above \(D_M\) stop everything.
In both: whether the better strain appears is a branching-process question, and deterministic models get it wrong.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
What computational epidemiology is for


Before an epidemic

Which interventions work?
Can an outbreak be contained?
How many vaccines should be stockpiled?


During an epidemic

Estimate transmission parameters
Interpret real-time trends
Assess the impact of interventions
Track new variants



Models are used for understanding (why does this happen?) and for prediction (what will happen?). This course is mostly about understanding.

title: Computational Epidemiology
section: All models are wrong, but some are useful
text:
All models are wrong, but some are useful
Every model trades off simplicity, accuracy and generality.

Toy models: simple and often solvable by hand. They build intuition for one new feature.
Realistic simulations: many details, used for “experiments” we cannot do. Hard to understand why they behave as they do.
Simple general models: capture the key features. They give simple results that explain a specific problem.


In your project, aim for the third kind. Start simple, then add one ingredient.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
A very short history

1760, Daniel Bernoulli: a mathematical model of smallpox, used to show that inoculation increases life expectancy.
1911, Ronald Ross: a model of malaria transmission. Reducing mosquitoes below a threshold eliminates the disease.
1927, Kermack & McKendrick: the SIR model. An epidemic stops before everyone is infected.


The core ideas we use today, thresholds and \(R_0\), come from these three.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Beginnings of formal epidemic modelling






Jenner/Bernoulli (smallpox), Snow (cholera, the first epidemiological map), Ross and Macdonald (malaria), Kermack and McKendrick, Anderson and May. Each step connects a disease to a modelling idea.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Compartments
Divide the population by disease status:



S
susceptible
can be infected


I
infected
infectious, can infect others


R
recovered (removed)
immune, or dead




We follow the proportions \(S(t)\), \(I(t)\) and \(R(t)\), with \(S + I + R = 1\), and ignore what happens inside each host. Lecture 3 opens that box.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Building the SIR model
How fast does \(I\) change?

Up: susceptibles meet infecteds at a rate proportional to \(S \cdot I\) (mass action), and a fraction of meetings transmits. Together: \(\beta S I\).


Down: each infected person recovers at rate \(\gamma\), so the mean infectious period is \(1/\gamma\). Together: \(\gamma I\).


\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta S I, \qquad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta S I - \gamma I, \qquad
\frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I
\]

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Where \(\beta S I\) comes from
Follow one infected person for a short time \(\Delta t\):


They make \(c\,\Delta t\) contacts (contact rate \(c\)).
A fraction \(S\) of those contacts are susceptible.
Each contact with a susceptible transmits with probability \(p\).



New infections caused by this person: \(c\,p\,S\,\Delta t\). With \(I\) infected people:
\[
\text{new infections in } \Delta t = \underbrace{c\,p}_{\beta}\; S\, I\, \Delta t
\]


Mass action assumes contacts are random: anyone can meet anyone. Lecture 4 drops this.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Where \(\gamma I\) comes from
Each infected person recovers with probability \(\gamma\,\Delta t\) in a short interval \(\Delta t\), independently of how long they have been infected.

For a group of \(I_0\) people infected at time 0, nobody new joining:
\[
\frac{dI}{dt} = -\gamma I \;\Rightarrow\; I(t) = I_0\, e^{-\gamma t}
\]



The fraction still infectious after time \(t\) is \(e^{-\gamma t}\): the infectious period is exponentially distributed.
Its mean is \(\int_0^\infty e^{-\gamma t}\,dt = 1/\gamma\).



This is a modelling choice. Real infectious periods are less variable. SEIR models and models with several I stages fix this (later today).

title: Computational Epidemiology
section: From time steps to differential equations
text:
From time steps to differential equations
Over a short step \(\Delta t\):
\[
I(t + \Delta t) = I(t) + \beta S I\, \Delta t - \gamma I\, \Delta t
\]

Rearrange and let \(\Delta t \to 0\):
\[
\frac{I(t + \Delta t) - I(t)}{\Delta t} = \beta S I - \gamma I
\;\xrightarrow{\;\Delta t \to 0\;}\;
\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta S I - \gamma I
\]


Every flow out of one compartment is a flow into another, so \(S + I + R = 1\) always:
\[
\frac{d}{dt}(S + I + R) = -\beta SI + (\beta SI - \gamma I) + \gamma I = 0
\]

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
What is a solution?
A solution is a set of functions \(S(t)\), \(I(t)\), \(R(t)\) that satisfy the equations for all \(t\).

One case we can solve by hand: at the very start, \(S \approx 1\):
\[
\frac{dI}{dt} \approx (\beta - \gamma)\, I
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
I(t) = I_0\, e^{(\beta - \gamma) t}
\]
The epidemic grows exponentially if \(\beta > \gamma\).


For the full SIR model there is no simple closed form. We solve it numerically, in a few lines of R (T1).

title: Computational Epidemiology
section: How a computer solves it: Euler’s method
text:
How a computer solves it: Euler’s method
Read the time-step equation backwards: from today’s state, compute tomorrow’s.

for (step in 1:n_steps) {
  dS <- -beta * S * I
  dI <-  beta * S * I - gamma * I
  S  <- S + dS * dt
  I  <- I + dI * dt
}











Smaller steps converge to the true solution. deSolve picks the step size for you. Full walkthrough: T0.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
One epidemic

Infections peak exactly when \(S\) drops to \(1/R_0\).

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Try it yourself (5 min)
Open T0 — Solving differential equations in R, section 5, and use run_sir() and plot_sir().
In pairs, predict first, then run:

What happens if you multiply \(\gamma\) or \(\beta\) by 2?
What happens if you multiply \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) by 2? Can you explain it?
What are the equilibria of the system, the states where nothing changes?
Are they stable? What would “stable” mean here?
What would you change in the model to make the disease persist?

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Quick check
What happens if we double both \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\)?

The epidemic has the same shape and the same final size, but runs twice as fast.
Only the ratio \(\beta/\gamma\) decides whether and how big. The values themselves only set the time scale.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
The basic reproduction number \(R_0\)

The expected number of secondary cases caused by one infected individual in a fully susceptible population.


One infected person infects at rate \(\beta S\) for an average time \(1/\gamma\). With \(S = 1\):
\[
R_0 = \frac{\beta}{\gamma}
\]


\(\dfrac{dI}{dt} > 0 \iff \beta S > \gamma \iff S > \dfrac{1}{R_0}\)
The epidemic can only grow while enough people are still susceptible.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
\(R_0\) by counting one generation
Take one step of the length of an infectious period, \(\Delta t = 1/\gamma\):

\[
I(t + 1/\gamma) \approx I + \beta S I \cdot \frac{1}{\gamma} - \gamma I \cdot \frac{1}{\gamma}
= \frac{\beta S}{\gamma}\, I
\]



The old infecteds are gone (they recovered).
Each was replaced by \(\beta S/\gamma\) new ones.

So each infected person is replaced by \(\beta S / \gamma\) others, which is \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma\) when \(S = 1\), and the effective reproduction number \(R_t = R_0\, S(t)\) later on.

title: Computational Epidemiology
section: How many get infected in the end?
text:
How many get infected in the end?
Divide \(dS/dt\) by \(dR/dt\), and time drops out:
\[
\frac{dS}{dR} = \frac{-\beta S I}{\gamma I} = -R_0\, S
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
S = S_0\, e^{-R_0 R}
\]

At the end, \(I = 0\), so the final size is \(Z = R_\infty = 1 - S_\infty\). With \(S_0 \approx 1\):
\[
\boxed{1 - Z = e^{-R_0 Z}}
\]



This has no closed form, but is easy to solve numerically (uniroot in R).
There is always a solution with \(Z > 0\) when \(R_0 > 1\). Not everyone gets infected: \(S_\infty > 0\).

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
How high is the peak?
Divide \(dI/dt\) by \(dS/dt\):
\[
\frac{dI}{dS} = \frac{\beta S I - \gamma I}{-\beta S I} = -1 + \frac{1}{R_0\, S}
\]

Integrate:
\[
I + S - \frac{\ln S}{R_0} = \text{const} = 1 \quad (\text{at the start: } S = 1, I = 0)
\]


The peak is at \(S = 1/R_0\), so
\[
\boxed{I_{\max} = 1 - \frac{1 + \ln R_0}{R_0}}
\qquad R_0 = 2: \; I_{\max} \approx 15\%
\]
This matches the simulation (0.1534 for both).

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
What herd immunity means
The idea: immune people do not just protect themselves. They also block chains of transmission to others.
An infected person meets others at random, and only a fraction \(S\) of contacts can be infected: \(R_t = R_0\, S\).
Once enough people are immune that \(R_t < 1\), chains still start but die out after a few infections. A large epidemic is no longer possible, and non-immune people are protected indirectly:
\[
\text{immune fraction} > \boxed{1 - \frac{1}{R_0}}
\]
Example: \(R_0 = 2.5\) needs 60% immune.

title: Computational Epidemiology
section: What herd immunity does not mean
text:
What herd immunity does not mean

It is a threshold for growth, not a force field. Above the threshold an introduced case still infects \(R_t/(1-R_t)\) people on average, and close to the threshold these chains are long. Chains shrink instead of growing. Below it, partial immunity still helps: at 50% immunity and \(R_0 = 2.5\), an unprotected person’s risk falls from 89% to 37%.



Reaching it through infection costs more than the threshold. The epidemic overshoots (next slide): at \(R_0 = 2\) the threshold is 50%, but about 80% get infected.




It assumes random mixing. National coverage above the threshold does not protect a cluster of unvaccinated people who mostly meet each other. Measles outbreaks in under-vaccinated communities are the classic example.




It is not a fixed number. It moves with \(R_0\): new variants, seasons and behaviour change it. Immunity can wane, so the immune fraction can slip back below the threshold.




Vaccines are not perfect. With efficacy \(E\), the coverage needed is \(v_c = (1 - 1/R_0)/E\). For measles (\(R_0 \approx 15\), \(E \approx 0.97\)) that is about 96%. If \(v_c > 1\), vaccination alone cannot do it.

title: Computational Epidemiology
section: Herd immunity threshold and final size
text:
Herd immunity threshold and final size

An unmitigated epidemic overshoots the herd immunity threshold: at \(R_0 = 2\), 50% are needed but about 80% get infected.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
\(R_0\) for real diseases



Disease
\(R_0\) (typical range)
Herd immunity threshold




Measles
12–18
92–94%


SARS-CoV-2 (ancestral strain)
about 2.5–3
about 60–67%


Seasonal influenza
about 1.3
about 23%




\(R_0\) is not a property of the pathogen alone. It depends on contact patterns, population density, season and behaviour. The same pathogen has different \(R_0\) in different places.
\(R_t\) is the reproduction number now, with immunity and interventions. Lecture 4 estimates it from data.

Measles range: Anderson & May 1991 (with the caveat from Guerra et al. 2017 that published values vary widely). Influenza: Biggerstaff et al. 2014, median about 1.28 for seasonal flu. Discussion: is “herd immunity” in public debate the same thing as the HIT here?

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
\(R_0\) and herd immunity across diseases





Source: Wikipedia, “Basic reproduction number”. Each value is a range from many studies, a reminder that \(R_0\) depends on the population as much as on the pathogen.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Equilibria
An equilibrium is a state where nothing changes: \(dS/dt = dI/dt = dR/dt = 0\).

For SIR: every state with \(I = 0\) is an equilibrium (any split between \(S\) and \(R\)).


Is it stable? Add a few infected individuals:

if \(S > 1/R_0\), they multiply: unstable;
if \(S < 1/R_0\), they die out: stable.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
The phase plane

Every trajectory peaks on the line \(S = 1/R_0\) and ends on the axis \(I = 0\).

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Adding births and deaths
New susceptibles arrive at rate \(\mu\), and everyone dies at rate \(\mu\):
\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = \mu - \beta S I - \mu S, \qquad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta S I - (\gamma + \mu) I
\]

Now \(R_0 = \beta/(\gamma + \mu)\), and there is a second equilibrium, the endemic one:
\[
S^* = \frac{1}{R_0}, \qquad I^* = \frac{\mu}{\beta}\,(R_0 - 1)
\]
It exists only if \(R_0 > 1\).

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Deriving the endemic equilibrium
Set both equations to zero.

From \(dI/dt = 0\), with \(I^* > 0\):
\[
\beta S^* = \gamma + \mu \quad\Rightarrow\quad S^* = \frac{\gamma + \mu}{\beta} = \frac{1}{R_0}
\]


From \(dS/dt = 0\):
\[
\mu - \beta S^* I^* - \mu S^* = 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
I^* = \frac{\mu\,(1 - S^*)}{\beta S^*} = \frac{\mu}{\beta}\,(R_0 - 1)
\]



\(I^* > 0\) only if \(R_0 > 1\).
\(I^*\) is proportional to \(\mu\): the birth rate of susceptibles sets how much infection the population can sustain.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Is the disease-free state stable?
Start at \(S = 1\), \(I = 0\) and add a few infecteds, \(I = \varepsilon\). While \(I\) is small, \(S \approx 1\):
\[
\frac{dI}{dt} \approx (\beta - \gamma - \mu)\, I = (\gamma + \mu)(R_0 - 1)\, I
\]


\(R_0 < 1\): \(I\) shrinks, so the disease-free state is stable.
\(R_0 > 1\): \(I\) grows, so it is unstable, and the system moves to the endemic state.



This is linearisation: near an equilibrium, keep only the terms that are linear in the small perturbation. It works for any model, and with several infected classes it gives the next-generation matrix.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text: The infection becomes endemic

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Vaccination threshold
Vaccinate a fraction \(v\) of newborns. They go straight to \(R\), so susceptibles are only produced at rate \(\mu(1 - v)\).

The disease-free state now has \(S = 1 - v\), and the linearisation becomes
\[
\frac{dI}{dt} \approx \big(\beta (1 - v) - \gamma - \mu\big)\, I
\]


Elimination requires \(R_0 (1 - v) < 1\):
\[
\boxed{v_c = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0}}
\]
This is the same number as the herd immunity threshold. For measles (\(R_0 \approx 15\)) it is about 93%, which is why measles returns as soon as coverage drops a few percent.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Beyond SIR: an exposed (latent) class


Many infections have a latent period: infected, but not yet infectious.
\[
\frac{dE}{dt} = \beta S I - \sigma E
\] \[
\frac{dI}{dt} = \sigma E - \gamma I
\]
Same \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma\), so the same final size. But the epidemic is slower and flatter.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
A real model: COVID-19 Scenarios





An SEIR model used for planning in 2020 (covid19-scenarios.org, Neher lab, University of Basel):

Three latent stages \(E^1 \to E^2 \to E^3\): the time to become infectious is no longer exponential but peaked (gamma-distributed). This is the standard fix for the “exponential period” problem from earlier.
Hospital (\(H\)), critical care (\(C\)), ICU overflow (\(O\)), death (\(D\)): the model predicts what hospitals need, not just cases.
Transmission modulated by interventions: \(\beta\) drops in steps when measures start.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
What such a model produces





Top: the transmission factor, stepped by interventions. Bottom: model curves (lines) fitted to weekly cases and deaths (dots). The efficacy of each intervention is an input chosen by the user, so every step in \(R\) is an assumption you can vary.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Vector-borne disease: West Nile virus





Birds are the reservoir and mosquitoes (Culex) the vector. Humans and horses are dead-end hosts: they get sick but do not transmit. © Christian Müller / Biogents.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
The bird–mosquito model







Only mosquitoes have demography (\(b_M\), \(d_M\)): they live weeks, birds years.
Frequency-dependent transmission, \(\beta S_B I_M / (S_B + I_B)\): each mosquito bites at a fixed rate.
Bird → mosquito → bird, so \(R_0 = \sqrt{R_{BM}\,R_{MB}}\) (next-generation definition).

Model from Wonham & Lewis (2008).

Ross’s insight still holds: reduce mosquitoes enough and R0 < 1. Infected mosquitoes stay infectious for life, so there is no recovery term for I_M.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Cholera: transmission through water







\(B\) is the concentration of Vibrio cholerae in the water. Infected people shed bacteria (\(\xi I\)), and the bacteria decay (\(\delta B\)).
Two routes of infection: from the water (\(b_B S B\)) and person-to-person (\(b_I S I\)).
The reservoir stores infection: the disease can come back after cases have disappeared. A saturating version, \(a\,B/(K+B)\), is used by Codeço (2001).


Same recipe every time: define compartments → write the flows → find \(R_0\) and the equilibria.

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Discussion

How useful is \(R_0\) as a single number?
What can go wrong when we compare \(R_0\) across diseases or countries?
Is “herd immunity” in public debate the same as the threshold \(1 - 1/R_0\)?

title: Computational Epidemiology
text:
Summary

Compartment models track proportions: \(S\), \(I\), \(R\), and more.
\(R_0 = \beta/\gamma\) decides whether an epidemic can start; \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) separately only set the time scale.
Infections peak at \(S = 1/R_0\); the epidemic overshoots the herd immunity threshold.
With births, the infection can persist at an endemic equilibrium.
Extensions follow one recipe: compartments → flows → \(R_0\) and equilibria.

Ask for explanations, not just answers. Have a Socratic dialogue with it.

title: Projects
text:
Project menu
These are starting points. You can combine them, change them or propose your own; the pitches are where you agree it with me. Each tutorial ends with more ideas under Project hooks.

A · Compartment models (start from T1)

Treatment. Add a treated compartment: treated individuals recover faster and may be less infectious. How effective must a drug be to change the epidemic peak?
Heterogeneity. Two groups that differ in susceptibility or in recovery rate. Does heterogeneity speed up or slow down spread, compared with a homogeneous population with the same average?
Seasonality. Let \(\beta\) oscillate over the year. When does seasonality produce multi-year cycles?
Vaccination strategy. Vaccinate newborns at coverage \(p\). Check the threshold \(p_c = 1 - 1/R_0\), then make it harder with waning immunity.



B · Branching processes and resistance (start from T2)

Dosing schedules. Make the stress \(r\) time-dependent: increasing, decreasing or cycling. Does a slow ramp-up of the antibiotic help resistance evolve?
Competition. Let the resistant mutant’s advantage depend on population density, e.g. strong only when sensitive cells are few. Does killing more sensitive cells help resistance?
Standing vs. new mutations. Start with a few resistant cells already present. Which matters more: pre-existing resistance or new mutations?
Superspreading. Replace Poisson offspring with an overdispersed (negative binomial) distribution. How does the takeoff probability change at the same \(R_0\)?



C · Strain evolution between hosts (start from T3)

Virulence evolution. Put a ladder of strains with different virulence on the trade-off curve. Does evolution find \(\alpha^* = \gamma + \mu\)?
Partial cross-immunity. Infection with strain 1 only partly protects against strain 2. When can two strains coexist?
Emergence during an epidemic. How early must a more transmissible variant appear to take over? Check the approximation with Gillespie simulations.



D · Within-host dynamics (start from T4)

Adherence. Patients miss doses. Model drug concentration as a function of time (pharmacokinetics). How much non-adherence pushes the patient into the selection window?
Combination therapy. Two drugs, where resistance to both needs two mutations. How much does combination therapy reduce the rescue probability?
Stochastic resistance. Replace the deterministic mutant with a branching process. When does resistance actually appear?



E · Space and individuals (start from T5)

Long-range jumps. Add a small probability of infecting a random cell anywhere. How many jumps turn a wave into exponential growth?
Spatial vaccination. Random vaccination vs. ring vaccination around cases, at the same number of doses.
Tumour on a grid. Cells divide into empty neighbouring sites, and a drug kills sensitive cells. Do resistant cells at the edge or in the core drive relapse?



F · Models meet data (start from T6)

Pick a dataset shipped with EpiEstim (e.g. SARS2003, Measles1861, Smallpox1972, Flu1918, mers_2014_15), estimate \(R_t\) and test how sensitive the answer is to the serial interval.
Know the truth. Simulate an epidemic with a lockdown (a drop in \(\beta\) on day 30). Does EpiEstim detect the drop, and how late?
Under-reporting. Only a fraction of cases is observed, and that fraction changes over time. What does that do to \(R_t\)?

title: When chance decides
text:
This morning’s SIR model says…
\(R_0 > 1 \;\Rightarrow\;\) an epidemic. Always.

But:

many imported cases never start an outbreak;
most new mutations are lost, even beneficial ones;
patients on antibiotics usually recover, even though resistance mutations arise all the time.



When numbers are small, chance decides. The ODE describes the average, but the average is not what happens to one rare lineage.

title: When chance decides
text:
Two puzzles, one question


Epidemic takeoff
One infected person arrives in a fully susceptible population with \(R_0 = 2\).
Will there be an epidemic?

Evolution of resistance
A bacterial infection is treated, and the population declines. A resistant mutant appears.
Will it save the population?








Both ask: does a rare lineage that grows on average escape extinction?







This is the frame for the whole lecture: first the epidemic, then resistance, then show it is the same formula.

title: When chance decides
section: Same model, simulated one event at a time
text:
Same model, simulated one event at a time


Gillespie algorithm: the same two events as the ODE (infection, recovery), drawn one at a time. Code is in T2. Black line: the ODE. Ask: what fraction do you expect to fizzle?

title: When chance decides
text:
The Gillespie algorithm
Same events and same rates as the ODE, but one event at a time, in a population of \(N\) individuals:



Event
Rate
Change




infection
\(a_1 = \beta S I / N\)
\(S - 1,\; I + 1\)


recovery
\(a_2 = \gamma I\)
\(I - 1,\; R + 1\)




Repeat:

Total rate \(a_0 = a_1 + a_2\).
Time to the next event: draw \(\tau \sim \text{Exponential}(a_0)\).
Which event: event \(i\) with probability \(a_i / a_0\).
Update the counts and the time, and go back to 1.

title: When chance decides
text:
Why exponential, and why \(a_i / a_0\)?
Each event type “waits” an exponential time with its own rate: \(P(\text{event } i \text{ not yet}) = e^{-a_i t}\).

When does the first event happen? Nothing has happened by time \(t\) if no event has happened:
\[
P(\text{nothing by } t) = e^{-a_1 t}\, e^{-a_2 t} = e^{-a_0 t}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad \tau \sim \text{Exponential}(a_0)
\]


Which event wins the race?
\[
P(\text{event 1 first}) = \int_0^\infty a_1 e^{-a_1 t}\, e^{-a_2 t}\, dt = \frac{a_1}{a_1 + a_2}
\]


The method is exact: no time step, no approximation. It is the same stochastic process whose average the ODE describes when \(N\) is large.

title: When chance decides
section: Early spread is a family tree
text:
Early spread is a family tree




Each case “gives birth” to new cases. The epidemic is a growing family tree.

Generation sizes multiply by about \(R_0\): exponential growth.
But each branch is random: whole branches can end by chance.
Early on, branches do not interfere, because susceptibles are not yet depleted.

Illustration: The Conversation, “How to flatten the curve of coronavirus: a mathematician explains” (2020).

title: When chance decides
text:
Branching processes
Early on almost everyone is susceptible, so infected individuals do not interact.

Each infected individual independently causes \(k\) new infections, with probability \(p_k\).
This is a Galton–Watson branching process: a family tree with random family sizes.


The same mathematics describes

surnames dying out (Watson & Galton, 1875),
beneficial mutations (Haldane, 1927),
resistant cells in a tumour or an infection,
transmission trees reconstructed from sequences (phylodynamics).

title: When chance decides
text:
Haldane’s trick
Let \(\eta\) be the probability that the lineage of one individual eventually dies out.

The lineage dies out if and only if all of its \(k\) offspring lineages die out. Each does so independently, with probability \(\eta\):
\[
\eta = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} p_k\, \eta^k \;=\; G(\eta)
\]


\(G\) is the probability generating function of the offspring distribution.

\(\eta = 1\) is always a solution.
If the mean \(G'(1) > 1\), there is a second solution \(\eta < 1\), and that is the answer.

title: When chance decides
section: Haldane step by step: Poisson offspring
text:
Haldane step by step: Poisson offspring
Offspring number \(k \sim \text{Poisson}(m)\), so \(p_k = e^{-m} m^k / k!\).

\[
G(\eta) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty e^{-m}\frac{m^k}{k!}\,\eta^k
= e^{-m} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(m\eta)^k}{k!}
\]


The sum is the exponential series, \(\sum_k x^k/k! = e^x\):
\[
G(\eta) = e^{-m}\, e^{m\eta} = e^{m(\eta - 1)}
\]


So the extinction probability solves
\[
\eta = e^{m(\eta - 1)}
\]
This has no closed-form solution. Solve it graphically or numerically.

title: When chance decides
text:
Solving \(\eta = G(\eta)\) graphically

Extinction probability: where \(G\) crosses the diagonal. Poisson gives \(\eta \approx 0.2\); geometric gives \(\eta = 1/2\).

title: When chance decides
section: Which offspring distribution does SIR have?
text:
Which offspring distribution does SIR have?
An infected person infects at rate \(\beta\) and recovers at rate \(\gamma\).
At every event, it is

an infection with probability \(q = \dfrac{\beta}{\beta + \gamma}\), or
recovery (the end) with probability \(1 - q\).


So the number of infections before recovery is geometric: \(p_k = (1 - q)\,q^k\), with mean \(\beta/\gamma = R_0\).
\[
G(\eta) = \frac{1}{1 + R_0(1-\eta)} \;\Rightarrow\; \eta = \frac{1}{R_0}
\qquad
\boxed{P(\text{takeoff}) = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0}}
\]

Common mistake (also in last year’s handout): assuming Poisson offspring for SIR. Poisson would be correct for a FIXED infectious period. Exponential infectious period plus Poisson infection gives a geometric distribution.

title: When chance decides
text:
Solving \(\eta = G(\eta)\) for SIR
Geometric offspring: \(p_k = (1-q)\,q^k\) with \(q = \beta/(\beta + \gamma)\).

\[
G(\eta) = (1 - q) \sum_{k=0}^\infty (q\eta)^k = \frac{1 - q}{1 - q\eta}
\qquad \text{(geometric series)}
\]


Set \(\eta = G(\eta)\) and multiply out:
\[
\eta\,(1 - q\eta) = 1 - q
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
q\eta^2 - \eta + (1 - q) = 0
\]


The two roots are \(\eta = 1\) and
\[
\eta = \frac{1 - q}{q} = \frac{\gamma}{\beta} = \frac{1}{R_0}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
P(\text{takeoff}) = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0}
\]
With \(I_0\) initial cases, each lineage must die out independently: \(P(\text{takeoff}) = 1 - R_0^{-I_0}\).

title: When chance decides
text:
Simulation vs. theory

Same mean, more variance, so fewer outbreaks take off.

title: When chance decides
text:
Superspreading
Most people infect few others, and a few infect many: the offspring distribution is overdispersed.
Lloyd-Smith et al. (2005) fitted negative binomial distributions with dispersion \(k\), where variance \(= R_0(1 + R_0/k)\). For SARS, \(k \approx 0.16\).

Consequences at the same \(R_0\):

Fewer introductions take off.
The ones that do take off grow explosively early on.
Targeting the few superspreaders is very effective.


Lloyd-Smith JO, Schreiber SJ, Kopp PE, Getz WM (2005) Nature 438:355-359. Good project: replace geometric by negative binomial in the takeoff simulation.

title: When chance decides
text:
Treatment selects for resistance



Bacteria: antibiotics kill sensitive cells. Rare resistant cells, already present or newly arising, take over.


Cancer: therapy shrinks the tumour, and resistant clones regrow it. The same process at the scale of cells.

title: When chance decides
text:
Treatment resistance is evolutionary rescue

Antibiotics, antivirals, chemotherapy: the pathogen or cancer population starts to decline.
A resistant mutant can rescue it from extinction.
This is the same process as evolutionary rescue in conservation biology (Gomulkiewicz & Holt 1995), with the opposite goal: here we want extinction.


Minimal model (discrete generations, Poisson offspring):




per generation





sensitive cells
mean offspring \(1 - r\)
decline: \(N_t = N(1-r)^t\)


resistant cells
mean offspring \(1 + s\)
growth


mutation
sensitive → resistant
probability \(u\) per new cell

title: When chance decides
section: Most new resistant lineages are lost
text:
Most new resistant lineages are lost

Drift phase (lost or not) → deterministic phase (growth like \(e^{st}\)).

title: When chance decides
text:
Establishment probability of one mutant
Poisson offspring with mean \(1 + s\) gives \(G(\eta) = e^{(1+s)(\eta - 1)}\). Write \(P = 1 - \eta\):
\[
1 - P = e^{-(1+s)P}
\]

For small \(s\), \(P\) is small too. Expand \(e^{-x} \approx 1 - x + x^2/2\):
\[
1 - P \approx 1 - (1+s)P + \tfrac{1}{2}(1+s)^2 P^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
P \approx \frac{2s}{(1+s)^2} \approx \boxed{2s}
\]


A resistant mutant with a 5% advantage is lost about 90% of the time.

title: When chance decides
text:
Counting mutants



Sensitive cells produced during the decline: \(\displaystyle\sum_t N(1-r)^t \approx \frac{N}{r}\)
Resistant mutants arising: \(\dfrac{Nu}{r}\)
Each establishes with probability \(2s\).
The number of successful mutants is roughly Poisson with mean \(2Nus/r\).


. . .
\[
P(\text{rescue}) \approx 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{2Nus}{r}\right)
\]
Orr & Unckless (2014)
The whole answer is one number: \(\theta = 2Nus/r\).

title: When chance decides
text: Simulation vs. theory

title: When chance decides
section: The two steps behind the formula
text:
The two steps behind the formula
Step 1: how many sensitive cells are ever produced? A geometric series:
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} N (1 - r)^t = N\,\frac{1 - r}{r} \approx \frac{N}{r}
\]
Halving the killing rate doubles the number of cells, and so doubles the number of mutation opportunities.

Step 2: why \(1 - e^{-\theta}\)? There are many mutants, each rare and each independently successful with probability \(2s\). The number of successes is then approximately Poisson with mean
\[
\theta = \underbrace{\frac{Nu}{r}}_{\text{mutants}} \times \underbrace{2s}_{\text{each establishes}}
\]
and rescue fails only if there are zero successes:
\[
P(\text{rescue}) = 1 - P(\text{0 successes}) = 1 - e^{-\theta}
\]

title: When chance decides
text:
What rescue looks like

The rescued populations make a U-shape: decline, a bottleneck, then recovery as the resistant lineage takes over.

title: When chance decides
text:
The three phases of rescue




Carlson, Cunningham & Westley (2014):

Decline: the old type dies out, while the adaptive allele (blue) rises from rare.
Danger zone: the population sits below a stochastic threshold. Chance can end it here, even if the adaptive allele has already spread.
Recovery: once adapted cells dominate, the population grows back.

Our branching-process calculation covers phases 1–2: does a rescue mutant arise and escape loss before the population is gone?

title: When chance decides
text:
What makes resistance more likely?
\[
\theta = \frac{2\,N\,u\,s}{r}
\]



Larger \(\theta\), more resistance
Clinical reading




large \(N\)
treat early, while the pathogen load is small


high \(u\)
mutagenic drugs and stress responses are bad news


large \(s\)
resistance that is cheap and effective


small \(r\)
slow killing: low doses, missed doses




Caveat: this assumes resistant and sensitive cells do not compete. If they do, killing sensitive cells helps the mutant (Day 2).

title: When chance decides
text:
Mutants that are already there
Before treatment, resistance usually carries a cost \(c\), and mutants sit at mutation–selection balance with frequency \(\approx u/c\).

Back-of-envelope:

pre-existing mutants \(\approx Nu/c\)
new mutants during the decline \(\approx Nu/r\)

So standing variation matters more than new mutations when \(c < r\): cheap resistance, fast killing.
See Orr & Unckless (2014) for the full treatment.

Hand-waving on purpose: each pre-existing mutant establishes with roughly the same 2s once treatment starts. Good project: start the T2 simulation with mutants at mutation-selection balance.

title: When chance decides
text:
Deriving the rule
Write the establishment probability as \(P = 1 - \eta\) and expand \(G\) around 1 (Taylor):
\[
G(1 - P) \approx 1 - G'(1)\,P + \tfrac{1}{2} G''(1)\,P^2
\]

Two facts about generating functions:
\[
G'(1) = E[k] = m, \qquad G''(1) = E[k(k-1)] = \sigma^2 + m^2 - m
\]


Insert into \(1 - P = G(1 - P)\):
\[
1 - P = 1 - mP + \tfrac{1}{2}(\sigma^2 + m^2 - m)P^2
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
P = \frac{2(m - 1)}{\sigma^2 + m(m - 1)} \;\approx\; \frac{2(m-1)}{\sigma^2}
\]
The last step uses \(m \approx 1\). For Poisson (\(\sigma^2 = m\)) the middle expression gives \(2s/(1+s)^2\), as before.

title: When chance decides
text:
The same formula, three times
For a rare lineage whose mean offspring number is just above 1:
\[
\boxed{P(\text{establish}) \;\approx\; \frac{2\,(\text{mean} - 1)}{\text{variance}}}
\]

text:
Where else this shows up

New variants arising during an epidemic (Day 2)
Resistance within a patient: the deterministic model always lets resistance win (Day 2)
Spatial structure: a mutant arising in a refuge vs. in the treated zone (Day 3)
Phylodynamics: birth–death models fitted to pathogen phylogenies to estimate \(R_t\) (Stadler et al. 2013)

title: When chance decides
text:
Summary

When numbers are small, chance decides and the ODE describes only the average.
Haldane: extinction probability solves \(\eta = G(\eta)\).
SIR has geometric offspring, so \(P(\text{takeoff}) = 1 - 1/R_0\).
A resistant mutant establishes with \(P \approx 2s\), and rescue happens with \(P \approx 1 - e^{-2Nus/r}\).
One rule: \(P \approx 2(\text{mean} - 1)/\text{variance}\).

title: Space, individuals and data
section: Two assumptions we have made all along
text:
Two assumptions we have made all along


Mass action
Every infected person can infect every susceptible person.
Today, part 1: what happens when contacts are local?

Known parameters
We picked \(\beta\), \(\gamma\) and \(R_0\).
Today, part 2: how do we get them from data, and how far can we trust them?


After the lecture: Pitch 3, first result. One figure per team.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
An epidemic on a grid
Each cell is one individual: susceptible, infected or recovered. In every time step:

a susceptible cell with \(k\) infected neighbours (up, down, left, right) is infected with probability \(1 - (1-p)^k\);
an infected cell recovers with probability \(q\).


This is an individual-based model: no compartments and no ODEs, just rules for each individual.
For comparison, the well-mixed version: the same \(p\), \(q\) and 4 contacts, but the contacts are drawn from the whole population.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
From rules to numbers
How long does a cell stay infected? It recovers with probability \(q\) per step, so the number of infectious steps is geometric, with mean \(1/q\).

Well mixed: per step, one infected cell infects about \(4p\) others (small \(p\)). Over \(1/q\) steps:
\[
R_0 \approx \frac{4p}{q}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \text{threshold at } p = q/4
\]


On the grid: what matters is the chance \(T\) that a given neighbour is ever infected. The neighbour escapes each step with probability \(1-p\), and the cell transmits for \(n\) steps with \(P(n) = q(1-q)^{n-1}\):
\[
T = 1 - \sum_{n \ge 1} q(1-q)^{n-1}(1-p)^n = 1 - \frac{q(1-p)}{1 - (1-q)(1-p)}
\]
We need \(T\) for the threshold in a few slides.

title: Space, individuals and data
text: Watch it spread

title: Space, individuals and data
section: The epidemic spreads as a wave
text:
The epidemic spreads as a wave

Infections can only happen at the front. Behind it, everyone has already recovered.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Local contacts kill exponential growth

Well mixed: \(e^{rt}\). Local: the front moves at constant speed \(c\), so cases grow like \(\pi c^2 t^2\).

title: Space, individuals and data
section: How fast does the front move?
text:
How fast does the front move?
In continuous space, with local growth rate \(r\) and diffusion \(D\) (the Fisher–KPP equation):
\[
\frac{\partial I}{\partial t} = r I + D \nabla^2 I
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
c = 2\sqrt{rD}
\]


Doubling the growth rate makes the wave only \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.4\times\) faster.
Classic examples: the Black Death in Europe, and rabies moving across a landscape at a roughly constant speed.
Long-range jumps (travel, trade) break this: patches far ahead of the front give accelerating spread.


Fisher 1937 (advance of advantageous genes), KPP 1937. Rabies in foxes: Murray, Stanley & Brown 1986. Project hook: add a small probability of jumping anywhere on the grid.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Where \(2\sqrt{rD}\) comes from
At the leading edge almost everyone is susceptible, so the equation is linear:
\[
\frac{\partial I}{\partial t} = r I + D \frac{\partial^2 I}{\partial x^2}
\]

Starting from a point source, the solution is spreading (diffusion) times growth:
\[
I(x, t) = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{4\pi D t}}\; \exp\!\left(r t - \frac{x^2}{4 D t}\right)
\]


The front is where \(I\) is still of order one, i.e. where the exponent is about zero:
\[
r t = \frac{x^2}{4 D t}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
x = 2\sqrt{rD}\; t
\]


So the front moves at constant speed \(c = 2\sqrt{rD}\). The infected area is a disc of radius \(ct\), so cumulative cases grow like \(\pi c^2 t^2\).

title: Space, individuals and data
section: Local contacts raise the epidemic threshold
text:
Local contacts raise the epidemic threshold

Dotted lines: well mixed, \(R_0 = 4p/q = 1\) at \(p = q/4\). Grid: bond percolation, where each neighbour is infected with probability ½, at \(p \approx q/(1+q)\).

Between the two lines each case would infect 1-2 neighbours on average in a fresh neighbourhood, yet the epidemic cannot cross the grid: neighbours share neighbours, and local depletion of susceptibles stops the wave. The q/(1+q) value comes from setting the per-neighbour transmissibility T = 1 - q(1-p)/(1-(1-q)(1-p)) equal to the square-lattice bond percolation threshold 1/2. It is an approximation, but it fits the simulation well.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Tumours grow in space






Waclaw et al. (2015): a 3D model of a growing tumour, with cells dividing into free space and occasionally migrating. Resistant clones are already present before treatment (a). The probability and timing of regrowth depend on the migration rate \(M\) (b, c).

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Space matters for resistance too
Within a host, drug concentrations are not uniform: tissues, abscesses, biofilms, tumours.


Drug gradients speed up resistance. Mutants can step up the gradient one mutation at a time, always next to an empty niche (Zhang et al. 2011; Hermsen et al. 2012).
Refuges where the drug is weak keep a population alive, and that population keeps supplying mutants.
Experiments: a slowly increasing drug concentration plus migration gives faster resistance (Perron et al. 2008; Bell & Gonzalez 2011).

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Gene flow and evolutionary rescue
Two habitats: an untreated refuge and a treated habitat, connected by migration \(m\).








Migration from refuge into treated habitat
Effect on rescue




brings sensitive cells in, so more mutants arise there
helps (demographic supply)


sends mutants back to the refuge, where they are at a disadvantage
hurts (loss of adapted lineages)





So rescue is most likely at intermediate migration, and only if the environment deteriorates slowly enough (Tomasini & Peischl 2018, 2020; Kirkpatrick & Peischl 2013).

This is the compressed version of ER deck slides 50-70. Pick one figure from Tomasini & Peischl to show here if time allows. Tumours: dispersal and cell turnover shape where resistant clones arise and how diverse a tumour is (Waclaw et al. 2015).

Experiment 1: yeast in a salt gradient






Yeast metapopulations on 96-well plates, with salt increasing from “south” to “north” (left). Populations were isolated or connected by local or global dispersal, and the environment deteriorated at different rates. Dispersal increased the number of rescued populations, most clearly in the “constant” treatment (right; Bell & Gonzalez 2011).

Experiment 2: bacteria and an antibiotic sink





Pseudomonas aeruginosa in an antibiotic “sink”, receiving immigrants from an untreated source at rates from 0% to 10% (symbols); the panels differ in how the antibiotic concentration increased. Higher immigration and a slow increase in antibiotic concentration gave faster resistance evolution (Perron et al. 2008).
