text:
A two-habitat model of rescue





Deme 1 deteriorates at time 0 and deme 2 at time \(\theta\), connected by migration. A rescue mutation is beneficial in the deteriorated habitat and harmful in the original one. Its fate is a two-type branching process (Tomasini & Peischl 2018).

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Rescue peaks at intermediate migration





Rescue probability against migration rate (points: simulations; lines: branching-process theory). When the environment deteriorates slowly across habitats, the curve has a maximum: some gene flow helps, too much swamps the mutants.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Many habitats, and continuous space


 
Island vs. stepping-stone migration between \(D\) demes (Tomasini & Peischl, preprint, doi 10.1101/2020.10.29.360842).


Continuous space: an individual-based simulation with a moving environmental boundary (Kirkpatrick & Peischl 2013). Migration has to be fine-tuned to the speed of environmental change.

title: Space, individuals and data
section: Inside a tumour: gradients from blood vessels
text:
Inside a tumour: gradients from blood vessels





Drug, oxygen and glucose fall off with distance from a blood vessel, so cells in different compartments experience different selection (doi 10.4137/CIN.S19338). Every tumour is a structured population with built-in refuges.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
What we actually observe
Not \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\), but case counts: noisy, delayed, and incomplete.
The question during an outbreak: is it growing or shrinking right now? That is, is \(R_t > 1\)?

The naive estimate, \(R_t \approx I_t / I_{t-\tau}\), raises three problems:

What is the right \(\tau\)? Infectiousness is spread over time.
Counts are random, so we need uncertainty.
Reporting changes over time.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
The renewal equation
Infections today are caused by infections over the past days, weighted by the serial interval \(w_s\):
\[
E[I_t] = R_t \,\Lambda_t, \qquad \Lambda_t = \sum_{s \ge 1} I_{t-s}\, w_s
\]

\(\Lambda_t\) is the total infectiousness currently out there.

title: Space, individuals and data
section: Where the renewal equation comes from
text:
Where the renewal equation comes from
Someone infected \(s\) days ago is still infectious, to a degree that depends on \(s\). Let \(w_s\) be the fraction of their total onward transmission that happens on day \(s\) (with \(\sum_s w_s = 1\)).

If each case causes \(R_t\) new cases in total, the cases from day \(t - s\) contribute
\[
I_{t-s} \cdot R_t \cdot w_s
\]
new cases today.


Sum over all past days:
\[
E[I_t] = R_t \sum_{s \ge 1} I_{t-s}\, w_s = R_t\, \Lambda_t
\]


In practice \(w_s\) is approximated by the serial interval: the time between symptom onsets of infector and infectee, which we can observe.

title: Space, individuals and data
section: Where does \(w_s\) come from? Viral shedding
text:
Where does \(w_s\) come from? Viral shedding




He et al. (2020) measured SARS-CoV-2 viral load in throat swabs of 94 patients, as Ct values: lower Ct means more virus.

Viral load is highest at symptom onset and declines over about 3 weeks.
This is similar across age, sex and severity.
So much transmission happens around or before symptoms, and isolating at symptom onset is too late.

title: Space, individuals and data
section: From transmission pairs to infectiousness profiles
text:
From transmission pairs to infectiousness profiles





He et al. (2020) combined 77 infector–infectee pairs with the incubation period to infer when infectors transmit. They estimated that about 44% of transmission happened before symptom onset. This is the \(w_s\) that goes into the renewal equation.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Bayesian estimation (Cori et al. 2013)
Assume \(I_t \sim \text{Poisson}(R\,\Lambda_t)\), with \(R\) constant over a window of \(\tau\) days and a gamma prior with shape \(a\) and scale \(b\).

The posterior is again a gamma distribution, with mean
\[
\hat R_t = \frac{a + \sum_{s = t-\tau+1}^{t} I_s}{1/b + \sum_{s = t-\tau+1}^{t} \Lambda_s}
\;\approx\; \frac{\text{cases in the window}}{\text{infectiousness in the window}}
\]


That is the whole method behind EpiEstim::estimate_R(). Everything else is choosing \(w_s\) and \(\tau\).

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Deriving the posterior
Likelihood: each day in the window is Poisson with mean \(R\Lambda_s\):
\[
L(R) = \prod_{s} \frac{(R\Lambda_s)^{I_s}\, e^{-R\Lambda_s}}{I_s!}
\;\propto\; R^{\sum I_s}\; e^{-R \sum \Lambda_s}
\]

Prior: gamma with shape \(a\) and scale \(b\): \(\;\pi(R) \propto R^{a-1} e^{-R/b}\).


Posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior:
\[
p(R \mid \text{data}) \;\propto\; R^{\,a + \sum I_s - 1}\; e^{-R\,(1/b + \sum \Lambda_s)}
\]
This is again a gamma distribution, with shape \(a + \sum I_s\) and rate \(1/b + \sum\Lambda_s\). Its mean is the formula on the previous slide.


Bonus: if only a constant fraction \(\rho\) of cases is reported, every \(I_s\) and every \(\Lambda_s\) is multiplied by \(\rho\), and \(\rho\) cancels in \(\sum I_s / \sum \Lambda_s\).

title: Space, individuals and data
section: Why the serial interval matters so much
text:
Why the serial interval matters so much
The data really tell us the growth rate \(r\). Turning \(r\) into \(R\) needs the generation interval (Wallinga & Lipsitch 2007). For an exponential interval with mean \(T_g\):
\[
R = 1 + r\,T_g
\]


The same growth with a shorter assumed interval gives an \(R\) closer to 1.
This matters most when \(R\) is far from 1, i.e. early on and after interventions.
Serial intervals are themselves estimated from transmission pairs, with their own uncertainty.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Deriving \(R = 1 + r\,T_g\)
During exponential growth, \(I_t = I_0 e^{rt}\). Put this into the renewal equation (continuous time, generation interval density \(g\)):
\[
I_0 e^{rt} = R \int_0^\infty I_0 e^{r(t - \tau)}\, g(\tau)\, d\tau
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
1 = R \int_0^\infty e^{-r\tau} g(\tau)\, d\tau
\]

For an exponential generation interval, \(g(\tau) = e^{-\tau/T_g}/T_g\):
\[
\int_0^\infty e^{-r\tau}\, \frac{e^{-\tau/T_g}}{T_g}\, d\tau = \frac{1}{1 + rT_g}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
R = 1 + r\,T_g
\]


Example: cases double every 5 days, so \(r = \ln 2/5 \approx 0.14\)/day. With \(T_g = 5\) days, \(R \approx 1.7\); with \(T_g = 2.6\) days, \(R \approx 1.4\). Same data, different \(R\).

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Other pitfalls







Issue
Effect on \(\hat R_t\)




Window length \(\tau\)
short: noisy; long: smooth but late


Constant under-reporting (only a fraction \(\rho\) of cases seen)
cancels: \(\rho\) appears in numerator and denominator


Changing reporting (more testing)
looks like growth: \(\hat R_t\) biased upwards


Reporting delays
the most recent days are incomplete, so \(\hat R_t\) looks like it is falling


Imported cases
counted as local transmission: \(\hat R_t\) too high




Rule of thumb: test your method on simulated data where you know the truth before trusting it on real data.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Beyond case counts

Hospitalisations and deaths: more reliable reporting, but a long delay after infection. Estimates lag by 2–3 weeks.
Wastewater: independent of testing behaviour, but needs calibration.
Pathogen sequences: the shape of the transmission tree carries information on \(R_t\).

Birth–death models fitted to phylogenies, e.g. the birth–death skyline (Stadler et al. 2013).
Lineages that branch fast mean a high \(R_t\).
This is the branching process from Day 1, read backwards from data.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Trees as data: birth–death models



Birth–death skyline: transmission (\(\lambda\)), becoming non-infectious (\(\mu\)) and sampling (\(\psi\)) rates change between time intervals. Fitting this to a sampled phylogeny gives \(R_e = \lambda/\mu\) through time (Stadler et al. 2013).


Multi-type: lineages can switch between types (e.g. locations or risk groups), each with its own rates (Barido-Sottani et al. 2020).

This is the branching process from Day 1, run backwards: from the tree to the rates.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Transmissible cancer in Tasmanian devils





Devil facial tumour disease spreads by biting: the cancer cells themselves are the pathogen. Patton et al. (2020) built a phylogeny from tumour genomes (C) and traced its spread across Tasmania (D).

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
From emergence to endemism





Birth–death phylodynamics on the tumour tree: in both clusters \(R_e\) was around 3–4 early on and has since dropped to about 1. This suggests the disease is becoming endemic rather than driving devils to extinction (Patton et al. 2020).

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Which interventions worked? The question


Haug et al. (2020) used \(R_t\) itself as data:

Interventions: 6,068 coded measures in 79 territories, March–April 2020 (CCCSL dataset; Desvars-Larrive et al. 2020).
Outcome: \(R_t\) estimated from case counts in each territory.
Methods: case-control analysis, LASSO regression, random forests and transformers. Each assigns every intervention an effect \(\Delta R_t\).

The hard part: many measures start at almost the same time, so their effects are entangled.


Example input: the Oxford Stringency Index and vaccination coverage over time.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Which interventions worked? The answer






Left: estimated effect ΔRt of each measure (most effective at the top). Right: agreement between the four methods (case-control, LASSO, random forest, transformer). Cancelling small gatherings, closing schools and border restrictions ranked among the most effective. Rankings depend on method and timing.

title: Space, individuals and data
text:
Summary

Local contacts: spread is a wave at constant speed \(c = 2\sqrt{rD}\), and cases grow like \(t^2\), not \(e^{rt}\).
Local contacts raise the threshold: \(R_0 > 1\) is not enough on a grid (percolation).
Space and resistance: gradients and refuges speed up resistance; migration has an optimum.
\(R_t\) from data: renewal equation; \(\hat R_t \approx\) cases ÷ infectiousness in the window.
The serial interval is an assumption, not a detail: \(R = 1 + rT_g\).

text:
library(deSolve)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 14))
The question. A mutant strain appears in a population where a resident strain is endemic. Recovery from either strain protects against both (complete cross-immunity). When does the mutant take over?

title: T3 — Strain invasion and virulence
section: Part A · Two strains competing for susceptibles
text:
Part A · Two strains competing for susceptibles
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt}   &= \mu - (\beta_1 I_1 + \beta_2 I_2) S - \mu S \\
\frac{dI_i}{dt} &= \beta_i S I_i - (\gamma_i + \mu) I_i \qquad i = 1, 2 \\
\frac{dR}{dt}   &= \gamma_1 I_1 + \gamma_2 I_2 - \mu R
\end{aligned}
\]
Invasion analysis. While the mutant (strain 2) is rare, the resident sits at its equilibrium \(S^* = 1/R_0^{(1)}\), where \(R_0^{(i)} = \beta_i/(\gamma_i + \mu)\). The mutant then grows at rate
\[
\lambda = \beta_2 S^* - (\gamma_2 + \mu) = (\gamma_2 + \mu)\left(\frac{R_0^{(2)}}{R_0^{(1)}} - 1\right).
\]
So the mutant invades if and only if it has the larger \(R_0\). It does not need to transmit faster per contact. Below, strain 2 has lower \(\beta\) but a longer infectious period.

two_strain <- function(t, x, p) {
  with(as.list(c(x, p)), {
    dS  <- mu - (b1 * I1 + b2 * I2) * S - mu * S
    dI1 <- b1 * S * I1 - (g1 + mu) * I1
    dI2 <- b2 * S * I2 - (g2 + mu) * I2
    dR  <- g1 * I1 + g2 * I2 - mu * R
    list(c(dS, dI1, dI2, dR))
  })
}
p   <- c(b1 = 3, g1 = 1, b2 = 2.4, g2 = 0.7, mu = 0.01)
R01 <- with(as.list(p), b1 / (g1 + mu))
R02 <- with(as.list(p), b2 / (g2 + mu))
c(R0_resident = R01, R0_mutant = R02)

R0_resident   R0_mutant 
   2.970297    3.380282 

# start: resident at equilibrium, one mutant in a million
S0  <- 1 / R01
I10 <- with(as.list(p), mu * (R01 - 1) / b1)
x0  <- c(S = S0, I1 = I10, I2 = 1e-6, R = 1 - S0 - I10 - 1e-6)
out <- as.data.frame(ode(x0, seq(0, 300, 0.5), two_strain, p))


long <- pivot_longer(out[, c("time", "I1", "I2")], -time, names_to = "strain", values_to = "I")
ggplot(long, aes(time, I, colour = strain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1e-8, NA)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(I1 = "#999999", I2 = "#E69F00"),
                      labels = c("resident", "mutant")) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Proportion infected (log)", colour = NULL)







Figure 1: A mutant with lower transmission rate but larger R0 replaces the resident.





Check the invasion rate against the formula:

early <- subset(out, time > 5 & time < 40)
c(predicted = with(as.list(p), (g2 + mu) * (R02 / R01 - 1)),
  observed  = unname(coef(lm(log(I2) ~ time, data = early))[2]))

predicted  observed

title: T3 — Strain invasion and virulence
section: Part B · Why not maximal transmission? The virulence trade-off
text:
Part B · Why not maximal transmission? The virulence trade-off
Suppose virulence \(\alpha\) (extra death rate of infected hosts) and transmission are linked, with \(\beta(\alpha) = b\sqrt{\alpha}\): a pathogen that replicates faster transmits better but kills its host sooner. Then
\[
R_0(\alpha) = \frac{b\sqrt{\alpha}}{\gamma + \mu + \alpha}, \qquad
\frac{dR_0}{d\alpha} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \alpha^* = \gamma + \mu .
\]
Combine this with Part A: if the strain with the largest \(R_0\) always wins, evolution should drive the pathogen to intermediate virulence \(\alpha^*\).

b <- 3; g <- 1; mu <- 0.01
alpha <- seq(0.01, 6, length.out = 300)
ggplot(data.frame(alpha, R0 = b * sqrt(alpha) / (g + mu + alpha)), aes(alpha, R0)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#E69F00") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = g + mu, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = expression("Virulence " * alpha), y = expression(R[0]))







Figure 2: With a transmission–virulence trade-off, R0 peaks at intermediate virulence α* = γ + μ (dashed).

title: T3 — Strain invasion and virulence
section: Part C · A variant emerging during one epidemic
text:
Part C · A variant emerging during one epidemic
There is no endemic equilibrium now, just a single SIR epidemic in a population of \(N\). Each new infection produces a mutant with probability \(u\), and the mutant has \(R_0^{(m)} > R_0\). As in T2, a mutant lineage arising at time \(t\) establishes with probability about \(1 - 1/(R_0^{(m)} S(t))\), but only if \(R_0^{(m)} S(t) > 1\). So
\[
P(\text{variant takes off}) \approx 1 - \exp\!\left(-\int_0^\infty u N \beta S(t) I(t)\,\max\!\left[0,\, 1 - \frac{1}{R_0^{(m)} S(t)}\right] dt\right).
\]
This is an approximation: it ignores that \(S\) keeps falling while the mutant lineage is still small. “Establishes” means the lineage escapes early extinction. Even a neutral variant (ratio 1) can do that if it arises early enough to ride the epidemic wave.

sir <- function(t, x, p) with(as.list(c(x, p)),
  list(c(-beta * S * I, beta * S * I - gamma * I, gamma * I)))
N <- 1e6; u <- 1e-6; gamma <- 1; R0 <- 1.5
dt  <- 0.05
epi <- as.data.frame(ode(c(S = 1 - 1e-5, I = 1e-5, R = 0), seq(0, 120, dt), sir,
                         c(beta = R0 * gamma, gamma = gamma)))

p_variant <- function(ratio) {
  R0m   <- ratio * R0
  p_est <- pmax(0, 1 - 1 / (R0m * epi$S))
  1 - exp(-sum(u * N * R0 * gamma * epi$S * epi$I * p_est * dt))
}
ratios <- seq(1, 3, by = 0.05)


ggplot(data.frame(ratios, P = sapply(ratios, p_variant)), aes(ratios, P)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#E69F00") +
  labs(x = expression("Relative fitness of variant  " * R[0]^{(m)} / R[0]),
       y = "P(variant lineage establishes)")







Figure 3: Probability that a variant arises and its lineage establishes during a single epidemic (N = 10^6, u = 10^-6, R0 = 1.5).

title: T5 — Spatial epidemics on a grid
text:
A cellular automaton
Each cell of an \(L \times L\) grid is one individual: susceptible (0), infected (1) or recovered (2). In every time step:

a susceptible cell with \(k\) infected neighbours (up, down, left, right) becomes infected with probability \(1 - (1 - p)^k\);
an infected cell recovers with probability \(q\).

This is an individual-based model: no compartment proportions and no ODEs, just rules for each individual. Counting neighbours with shifted copies of the grid is fast, even in R.

shift <- function(m, dr, dc) {                 # shift a matrix, filling with 0
  L <- nrow(m); out <- matrix(0, L, L)
  rs <- max(1, 1 + dr):min(L, L + dr); cs <- max(1, 1 + dc):min(L, L + dc)
  out[rs, cs] <- m[rs - dr, cs - dc]
  out
}

ca_sir <- function(L = 101, p = 0.3, q = 0.2, steps = 150, mixed = FALSE) {
  grid <- matrix(0L, L, L)
  grid[ceiling(L / 2), ceiling(L / 2)] <- 1L   # one infected cell in the middle
  snaps <- list(); cum <- numeric(steps)
  for (t in 1:steps) {
    inf <- (grid == 1) * 1
    k <- if (mixed) {
      4 * mean(inf)                            # well-mixed: 4 contacts drawn from everyone
    } else {
      shift(inf, 1, 0) + shift(inf, -1, 0) + shift(inf, 0, 1) + shift(inf, 0, -1)
    }
    new_inf <- grid == 0 & runif(L^2) < 1 - (1 - p)^k
    recover <- grid == 1 & runif(L^2) < q
    grid[new_inf] <- 1L
    grid[recover] <- 2L
    cum[t] <- sum(grid > 0)
    if (t %in% c(20, 50, 80)) snaps[[as.character(t)]] <- grid
  }
  list(snaps = snaps, cum = cum)
}

local_run <- ca_sir()


snap_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(local_run$snaps), function(t) {
  g <- local_run$snaps[[t]]
  data.frame(x = rep(1:ncol(g), each = nrow(g)), y = rep(1:nrow(g), ncol(g)),
             state = factor(c(g), levels = 0:2, labels = c("S", "I", "R")),
             time = paste("t =", t))
}))
snap_df$time <- factor(snap_df$time, levels = paste("t =", names(local_run$snaps)))
ggplot(snap_df, aes(x, y, fill = state)) +
  geom_raster() + facet_wrap(~time) + coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(S = "grey92", I = "#E69F00", R = "#56B4E9")) +
  theme_void(base_size = 14) + labs(fill = NULL)







Figure 1: The epidemic spreads as a ring: infected cells (orange) form a travelling front, with recovered cells (blue) behind it.

title: T5 — Spatial epidemics on a grid
text:
Waves grow slowly
With mass action, cases grow exponentially at first. On a grid, new infections can only happen at the front of the epidemic. The front moves at a roughly constant speed, so the infected area grows like \(t^2\).
To compare like with like, we run the same model with the 4 contacts drawn from the whole population instead of the neighbours (mixed = TRUE). This has the same \(p\), the same \(q\) and the same number of contacts.

mixed_run <- ca_sir(mixed = TRUE)
growth <- rbind(data.frame(time = 1:150, cum = local_run$cum, contacts = "local (grid)"),
                data.frame(time = 1:150, cum = mixed_run$cum, contacts = "well mixed"))
ggplot(growth, aes(time, cum, colour = contacts)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`local (grid)` = "#E69F00", `well mixed` = "grey40")) +
  labs(x = "Time step", y = "Cumulative infections (log)", colour = NULL)







Figure 2: Cumulative infections: well-mixed contacts (grey) grow exponentially; local contacts (orange) grow like t². Log scale.





(The well-mixed run can die out by chance in its first steps. If it does, change the seed, and remember T2.)

title: T0 — Solving differential equations in R
text:
library(deSolve)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 14))
pal <- c(S = "#999999", I = "#E69F00", R = "#56B4E9")
The goal. A differential equation tells you how fast something changes right now. Solving it means finding the whole curve over time. For most models, including SIR, there is no formula for that curve, so we let the computer build it step by step. This tutorial shows how that works, so that deSolve is not a black box.

title: T0 — Solving differential equations in R
section: 1 · A model we can solve by hand
text:
1 · A model we can solve by hand
At the start of an epidemic almost everyone is susceptible, and the number infected grows at a constant per-capita rate \(r = \beta - \gamma\):
\[
\frac{dI}{dt} = r\, I \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad I(t) = I_0\, e^{rt}.
\]
This is our test case: we know the exact answer, so we can check the computer against it.

title: T0 — Solving differential equations in R
section: 2 · Euler’s method: one small step at a time
text:
2 · Euler’s method: one small step at a time
The derivative says how much \(I\) changes in a short time \(\Delta t\):
\[
I(t + \Delta t) \approx I(t) + \underbrace{r\, I(t)}_{dI/dt}\, \Delta t .
\]
Start at \(I_0\), apply this rule over and over, and you get the whole curve.

euler_growth <- function(r, I0, tmax, dt) {
  n <- round(tmax / dt)
  I <- numeric(n + 1); I[1] <- I0
  for (k in 1:n) {
    I[k + 1] <- I[k] + r * I[k] * dt     # today's value + change over one step
  }
  data.frame(time = (0:n) * dt, I = I)
}


r <- 0.5; I0 <- 1; tmax <- 10
exact <- data.frame(time = seq(0, tmax, 0.01), I = I0 * exp(r * seq(0, tmax, 0.01)))
steps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 0.5, 0.1), function(dt)
  cbind(euler_growth(r, I0, tmax, dt), dt = paste("dt =", dt))))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = exact, aes(time, I), linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_line(data = steps, aes(time, I, colour = dt), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = subset(steps, dt == "dt = 1"), aes(time, I, colour = dt), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9")) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "I", colour = NULL)







Figure 1: Euler’s method with three step sizes (coloured) against the exact solution (black). Big steps fall behind, because the growth rate is only updated at the start of each step.





How fast does the error shrink? Compare the Euler value at \(t = 10\) with the exact one for many step sizes:

dts <- 2^-(0:8)
err <- sapply(dts, function(dt) {
  e <- euler_growth(r, I0, tmax, dt)
  abs(tail(e$I, 1) - I0 * exp(r * tmax)) / (I0 * exp(r * tmax))
})
ggplot(data.frame(dt = dts, err = err), aes(dt, err)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#56B4E9", linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#56B4E9") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Step size dt (log)", y = "Relative error at t = 10 (log)")







Figure 2: Relative error of Euler’s method at t = 10. On a log–log scale the slope is 1: halving the step halves the error (a ‘first-order’ method).











Rule of thumb



The step must be small compared with the fastest time scale in the model. Here that is \(1/r = 2\) time units. At \(t = 10\), Euler with \(\Delta t = 1\) is off by about 60%, with \(\Delta t = 0.1\) by about 11%, and with \(\Delta t = 0.01\) by about 1%. Errors also accumulate over time, so long simulations need smaller steps.

title: T0 — Solving differential equations in R
text:
3 · Euler for the SIR model
Exactly the same idea, now with three equations updated together:
\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta S I, \qquad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta S I - \gamma I, \qquad
\frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I .
\]

euler_sir <- function(beta, gamma, S0 = 1 - 1e-4, I0 = 1e-4, tmax = 40, dt = 0.1) {
  n <- round(tmax / dt)
  out <- matrix(NA_real_, n + 1, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("time", "S", "I", "R")))
  S <- S0; I <- I0; R <- 1 - S0 - I0
  out[1, ] <- c(0, S, I, R)
  for (k in 1:n) {
    dS <- -beta * S * I               # compute ALL rates from the current state first,
    dI <-  beta * S * I - gamma * I
    dR <-  gamma * I
    S <- S + dS * dt                  # ... then update all compartments together
    I <- I + dI * dt
    R <- R + dR * dt
    out[k + 1, ] <- c(k * dt, S, I, R)
  }
  as.data.frame(out)
}







A classic bug



If you update S first and then compute dI with the new S, the compartments are no longer updated consistently and \(S + I + R\) drifts away from 1. Always compute all rates first, then update. Check: rowSums(euler_sir(2, 1)[, c("S", "I", "R")]) should be 1 everywhere.

title: T0 — Solving differential equations in R
text:
4 · The same model with deSolve
deSolve::ode() does the stepping for you, with a much better method (lsoda) that chooses the step size automatically. You only write down the right-hand side of the equations:

sir <- function(t, state, p) {
  with(as.list(c(state, p)), {
    dS <- -beta * S * I
    dI <-  beta * S * I - gamma * I
    dR <-  gamma * I
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}


ds <- as.data.frame(ode(c(S = 1 - 1e-4, I = 1e-4, R = 0), seq(0, 40, 0.1), sir,
                        c(beta = 2, gamma = 1)))
eu <- rbind(cbind(euler_sir(2, 1, dt = 0.5), method = "Euler, dt = 0.5"),
            cbind(euler_sir(2, 1, dt = 0.1), method = "Euler, dt = 0.1"))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = ds, aes(time, I), linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_line(data = eu, aes(time, I, colour = method), linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#56B4E9")) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Infected I", colour = NULL)







Figure 3: Infected fraction from your own Euler solver (dashed, dt = 0.5 and 0.1) and from deSolve (solid black).





From now on we use deSolve. But you now know what it does: many small steps from “rate of change now” to “state a moment later”.

title: T0 — Solving differential equations in R
text:
5 · Explore the model
Two helpers so you can try many parameter values quickly:

run_sir <- function(beta, gamma, S0 = 1 - 1e-4, I0 = 1e-4, tmax = 40) {
  as.data.frame(ode(c(S = S0, I = I0, R = 1 - S0 - I0), seq(0, tmax, 0.05), sir,
                    c(beta = beta, gamma = gamma)))
}
plot_sir <- function(out, title = NULL) {
  long <- pivot_longer(out, -time, names_to = "compartment", values_to = "x")
  ggplot(long, aes(time, x, colour = compartment)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
    labs(x = "Time", y = "Proportion", colour = NULL, title = title)
}


plot_sir(run_sir(beta = 2, gamma = 1), "beta = 2, gamma = 1")







Figure 4: Baseline: beta = 2, gamma = 1, so R0 = 2.





Work through these questions in pairs. Write down your prediction before you run the code.

Q1 · Multiply \(\gamma\) or \(\beta\) by 2. What happens?

plot_sir(run_sir(beta = 4, gamma = 1), "beta doubled")
plot_sir(run_sir(beta = 2, gamma = 2), "gamma doubled")







Check your answer





Doubling \(\beta\) doubles \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma\) to 4: the epidemic is faster, higher, and infects almost everyone (final size about 98%). Doubling \(\gamma\) halves \(R_0\) to 1: the epidemic does not take off at all, because each case is now replaced by exactly one new case.





Q2 · Multiply \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) by 2. Can you explain the result?

a <- run_sir(beta = 2, gamma = 1)
b <- run_sir(beta = 4, gamma = 2)
plot_sir(b, "both doubled")
max(a$I); max(b$I)                  # peak height
tail(a$R, 1); tail(b$R, 1)          # final size







Check your answer





Same peak height, same final size, but everything happens twice as fast. Only the ratio \(\beta/\gamma = R_0\) decides whether and how big. The absolute values set the time scale. Mathematically: with the rescaled time \(\tau = \gamma t\) the equations depend on \(R_0\) only. Check it by plotting both runs against time * gamma: the curves fall on top of each other.

a <- run_sir(beta = 2, gamma = 1); b <- run_sir(beta = 4, gamma = 2)
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = a, aes(time * 1, I, colour = "beta = 2, gamma = 1"), linewidth = 2) +
  geom_line(data = b, aes(time * 2, I, colour = "beta = 4, gamma = 2"), linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "black")) +
  labs(x = "Rescaled time  gamma * t", y = "I", colour = NULL)




Both runs plotted against rescaled time gamma * t collapse onto one curve.









Q3 · What are the equilibria, the states where nothing changes?
Hint: set \(dS/dt = dI/dt = dR/dt = 0\) and solve. Then check numerically by running the model for a long time:

out <- run_sir(beta = 2, gamma = 1, tmax = 200)
tail(out, 1)                                        # where does it end up?
sir(0, unlist(tail(out, 1)[, -1]), c(beta = 2, gamma = 1))   # rates at the end: all ~ 0?







Check your answer





All three rates are zero exactly when \(I = 0\). So every state without infecteds is an equilibrium, whatever the split between \(S\) and \(R\). There is a whole line of equilibria, not a single point. The epidemic ends on this line at \(S_\infty = 1 - Z\), where \(Z\) is the final size.





Q4 · Are these equilibria stable? What would “stable” mean here?
Stable means: after a small disturbance, the system returns. Disturb a disease-free state by adding a few infecteds, once with many and once with few susceptibles:

plot_sir(run_sir(beta = 2, gamma = 1, S0 = 0.9, I0 = 1e-4), "S0 = 0.9")
plot_sir(run_sir(beta = 2, gamma = 1, S0 = 0.3, I0 = 1e-4), "S0 = 0.3")







Check your answer





With \(S = 0.9 > 1/R_0 = 0.5\) the few infecteds start an epidemic: that equilibrium is unstable. With \(S = 0.3 < 1/R_0\) they die out: stable. So the line of equilibria is unstable above \(S = 1/R_0\) and stable below it. This is exactly the herd immunity threshold from the lecture.





Q5 · What would you change in the model so the disease persists?






Check your answer





New susceptibles must keep arriving. Add births and deaths at rate \(\mu\): \(dS/dt = \mu - \beta S I - \mu S\) and \(dI/dt = \beta S I - (\gamma + \mu) I\). Then there is an endemic equilibrium with \(S^* = 1/R_0\) and \(I^* > 0\). Other routes: waning immunity (\(R \to S\)), or immigration of infecteds. T1 solves the model with births and deaths.

title: T0 — Solving differential equations in R
text:
6 · Your turn: an SEIR model
Add an exposed (latent) class: infected but not yet infectious, leaving at rate \(\sigma\).
\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta S I, \quad
\frac{dE}{dt} = \beta S I - \sigma E, \quad
\frac{dI}{dt} = \sigma E - \gamma I, \quad
\frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I
\]

Write a function seir(t, state, p) in the style of sir() above, and solve it with ode().
Compare with SIR at the same \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\). What changes: the final size, the peak, the timing?
Optional: solve it with your own Euler loop too. Which step size do you need when \(\sigma\) is large (a short latent period)?

title: T6 — Estimating R_t from incidence data
text:
library(EpiEstim)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 14))
set.seed(42)
The question. During an epidemic we observe daily case counts, not \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\). How do we get the reproduction number from them, and how far can we trust the answer?

title: T6 — Estimating R_t from incidence data
text:
The renewal equation
Let \(I_t\) be the number of new cases on day \(t\), and \(w_s\) the serial interval distribution, i.e. the probability that a secondary case shows symptoms \(s\) days after its infector. Then the expected number of new cases is
\[
E[I_t] = R_t \sum_{s \ge 1} I_{t-s}\, w_s .
\]
Cori et al. (2013) assume \(I_t\) is Poisson, \(R_t\) is constant within a sliding window, and \(R_t\) has a gamma prior. The posterior of \(R_t\) is then again a gamma distribution. This is what EpiEstim::estimate_R computes.

title: T6 — Estimating R_t from incidence data
section: Part A · A real outbreak: H1N1 in a school, 2009
text:
Part A · A real outbreak: H1N1 in a school, 2009

data(Flu2009)
head(Flu2009$incidence)

       dates I
1 2009-04-27 1
2 2009-04-28 1
3 2009-04-29 0
4 2009-04-30 2
5 2009-05-01 5
6 2009-05-02 3


The serial interval for influenza has mean 2.6 days and SD 1.5 days (Ferguson et al. 2005, Nature).

res_flu <- estimate_R(Flu2009$incidence, method = "parametric_si",
                      config = make_config(mean_si = 2.6, std_si = 1.5))
plot(res_flu, what = "R", legend = FALSE)







Figure 1: R_t for the 2009 H1N1 school outbreak (7-day sliding windows, parametric serial interval).

title: T6 — Estimating R_t from incidence data
section: Part B · Does EpiEstim recover the truth?
text:
Part B · Does EpiEstim recover the truth?
With real data we never know the true \(R_t\). So we simulate an epidemic in which we do know it, and test the method on that.
We use the Gillespie SIR model from T2 with \(N = 2000\), \(R_0 = 2\) and a mean infectious period of 5 days (\(\gamma = 0.2\)/day). In this model the true reproduction number is \(R_t = R_0\, S(t)/N\). The infectious period is exponential, so the generation interval is also exponential, with mean and SD both \(1/\gamma = 5\) days.

sim_epidemic <- function(N, beta, gamma, I0) {
  S <- N - I0; I <- I0; t <- 0
  inf_times <- rep(0, I0); S_track <- data.frame(time = 0, S = S)
  while (I > 0) {
    a_inf <- beta * S * I / N; a_rec <- gamma * I
    t <- t + rexp(1, a_inf + a_rec)
    if (runif(1) < a_inf / (a_inf + a_rec)) {
      S <- S - 1; I <- I + 1
      inf_times <- c(inf_times, t)
      S_track <- rbind(S_track, data.frame(time = t, S = S))
    } else I <- I - 1
  }
  list(inf_times = inf_times, S_track = S_track)
}

N <- 2000; gamma <- 0.2; R0 <- 2
sim <- sim_epidemic(N, beta = R0 * gamma, gamma = gamma, I0 = 10)

days      <- 0:ceiling(max(sim$inf_times))
incidence <- as.vector(table(factor(floor(sim$inf_times), levels = days)))
true_Rt   <- data.frame(day = days,
                        Rt = R0 * approx(sim$S_track$time, sim$S_track$S, xout = days,
                                         method = "constant", rule = 2)$y / N)

Now we estimate \(R_t\) twice: with the correct serial interval (mean 5, SD 5), and with the influenza one from Part A (mean 2.6, SD 1.5), as if we had borrowed it from the wrong disease.

estimate_with <- function(mean_si, std_si, label) {
  T_end <- length(incidence)
  cfg <- make_config(mean_si = mean_si, std_si = std_si,
                     t_start = 2:(T_end - 6), t_end = 8:T_end)
  r <- estimate_R(incidence, method = "parametric_si", config = cfg)$R
  data.frame(day = r$t_end - 3 - 1,            # window centre, as a day since start
             mean = r$`Mean(R)`, lo = r$`Quantile.0.025(R)`, hi = r$`Quantile.0.975(R)`,
             si = label)
}
est <- rbind(estimate_with(5,   5,   "correct SI (mean 5 d)"),
             estimate_with(2.6, 1.5, "wrong SI (mean 2.6 d)"))
est <- filter(est, day <= max(days) - 10)       # drop the noisy tail


ggplot(est, aes(day, mean, colour = si, fill = si)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_line(data = filter(true_Rt, day <= max(est$day)), aes(day, Rt),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#56B4E9", "#D55E00"), aesthetics = c("colour", "fill")) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = expression(R[t]), colour = NULL, fill = NULL)







Figure 2: Estimated R_t (ribbons: 95% credible intervals) against the true R_t of the simulation (black). The wrong serial interval pulls the estimates towards 1.





Why it goes wrong. Growth rate \(r\) and reproduction number are linked through the generation interval. For an exponential interval with mean \(T_g\), \(R = 1 + r T_g\). Assuming a shorter serial interval means the same observed growth is read as a smaller \(R\). Shorter generations need fewer secondary cases each to grow equally fast.
